## business-model / 03_segment-map.md

_Source: `business-model/03_segment-map.md`_

# Segment Map — DHER

Basis: Delivery Hero SE (XTRA:DHER), Prime Standard / Frankfurt Stock Exchange, reports under IFRS as adopted by the EU, in EUR, fiscal year ending Dec-31. All figures below are FY2024 (year ended Dec-31-2024) unless stated otherwise, sourced from the audited FY2024 Annual Report (published Apr 25, 2025) — the most recent Tier-1 filing in the pool. No FY2025 audited annual report or `ciq_facts.json` sidecar exists in this pool (confirmed absent); FY2025 figures cited below are explicitly labeled as Capital IQ workbook / earnings-transcript sourced (Tier 5/6) and used only as a directional cross-check, per `analyses/DHER_2026-08-12/business-model/00_data-triage.md`.

## 1. Segment Table

Delivery Hero manages itself as five reportable segments: four regional online-marketplace ("platform") segments plus one cross-regional operating-model segment (Integrated Verticals) that spans multiple regions [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, Note A.3 "Segments", p.100].

| Segment | What It Does | Revenue Share | Profit Share | Margin Quality | Capital Intensity | Cyclicality | Main Risk |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| MENA | Online food-delivery/marketplace (talabat, Hungerstation, InstaShop) in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, UAE; plus Yemeksepeti in Türkiye [FY24 AR, p.100–101] | 27.6% (€3,527.8m of €12,796.4m Total Segment Revenue) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | 68.3% (€472.9m of €692.5m Group Adj. EBITDA) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | High — 13.4% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue in 2024, up from 11.3% in 2023; "MENA segment performed significantly better than expected" [FY24 AR, p.4, p.105–106] | Not disclosed (no segment-level capex in filing); qualitatively marketplace/commission-based, not warehouse-heavy — Inference, not from filings | Mid — Inference, not from filings; no segment-level cyclicality analysis in filing | ~20% of talabat's economics belong to public minority shareholders after its Dec-10-2024 Dubai Financial Market listing (DH retained an 80% stake) — the segment table consolidates 100% of talabat's result, so the 68.3% profit share overstates DHER shareholders' claim on MENA cash flow. Türkiye hyperinflation (IAS 29) also distorts YoY comparability [FY24 AR, p.4 (footnote), p.106] |
| Asia | Foodpanda marketplace across Bangladesh, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand; Baemin (Woowa) in South Korea [FY24 AR, p.100–101] | 31.8% (€4,071.9m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | 55.6% (€385.1m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | Mid — 9.5% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue, essentially flat vs. 10.3% in 2023 despite +9.2% revenue growth; GMV fell −7.7% [FY24 AR, p.4, p.105] | Not disclosed; Inference, not from filings | Mid — Inference, not from filings | "GMV of the Asia segment declined (−7.7%), mainly driven by rising competition in certain regions"; adjusted EBITDA "remained flat year-over-year, mainly due to the effects of the competitive environment" [FY24 AR, p.105–106] — the only segment where GMV fell in FY2024 |
| Integrated Verticals | Own-warehouse quick commerce ("Dmarts") — DH acts as principal (buys and resells inventory) rather than commission agent; operated in 48 countries [FY24 AR, p.101] | 21.2% (€2,709.8m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | −14.3% (−€98.7m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | Low — margin of −3.6% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue, improved from −10.2% in 2023; "underscores progress towards breakeven," not yet achieved [FY24 AR, p.4, p.106] | High — Inference, not from filings: only segment where DH holds inventory and operates its own warehouses (principal model), unlike the commission-based marketplace model of the four platform segments; no segment capex figure is disclosed to confirm the magnitude | Mid — Inference, not from filings | Still a −€98.7m drag on Group Adj. EBITDA despite +27.5% revenue growth; inventory-heavy "principal" model with thinner unit economics than the marketplace segments, in a sub-sector (quick commerce) that has seen multiple competitor failures/consolidations industry-wide (context, not filing-sourced) |
| Europe | Glovo, foodora, efood, foody marketplace across ~25 European countries; also includes Glovo's Africa (Ivory Coast, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, Tunisia, Uganda) and Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan) operations, bundled into this segment [FY24 AR, p.100–101] | 14.8% (€1,891.9m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | −11.1% (−€77.0m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | Low — margin of −4.1% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue, improved from −11.0% in 2023, but still loss-making [FY24 AR, p.4] | Not disclosed; Inference, not from filings | Mid — Inference, not from filings | Rider-classification/labor regulation risk: additional provisions "for rider-related reclassification risks in Italy" were the specific reason cited for the Group missing its own FY2024 Adj. EBITDA target range (€725–775m guided vs. €692.5m actual); Glovo is moving to an employment-based rider model in Spain in 2025 "to reduce future legal uncertainty" [FY24 AR, p.9, p.105–106] |
| Americas | PedidosYa marketplace across Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Venezuela [FY24 AR, p.100–101] | 7.3% (€939.6m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | 1.5% (€10.3m) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4] | Low — thin 1.1% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue margin, though a sharp swing from −7.7% in 2023; "Americas segment reaching a positive adjusted EBITDA in Q3 and Q4 2024" [FY24 AR, p.4, p.106] | Not disclosed; Inference, not from filings | Mid — Inference, not from filings; Argentina hyperinflation (IAS 29) adjustments reduce comparability of reported growth [FY24 AR, p.4 (footnote)] | Smallest segment by both revenue and profit; profitability only turned positive in H2 2024 and remains thin — one bad quarter could push it back to loss, and results carry Argentine hyperinflation adjustments [FY24 AR, p.4 (footnote), p.106] |

**Revenue-share note:** the five segment-revenue figures above sum to €13,141.0m — 102.7% of the disclosed "Total Segment Revenue" of €12,796.4m. The 2.7-point excess is the company's own disclosed intersegment-consolidation adjustment of −€344.5m ("mainly due to intersegment consolidation adjustments for services charged by the Platform segment to the Integrated Verticals segment") [FY24 AR, p.4, "Notes"]. This is disclosed, not an extraction error — flagged rather than silently forced to 100%. A cleaner, IFRS-clean cross-check is the company's own "Segment share of Group GMV" pie chart, which sums to exactly 100% (Asia 48%, MENA 26%, Europe 18%, Americas 8%; Integrated Verticals GMV is embedded within the four platform segments' GMV and shown separately "for illustrative purposes only," so it is excluded from this specific chart) [FY24 AR, p.4–5]. Profit shares (Adj. EBITDA) sum to 100.0% with no such elimination issue.

**"Total Segment Revenue" vs. IFRS "Revenue":** the segment table above uses Total Segment Revenue (€12,796.4m for FY2024), the company's own primary segment KPI, defined as revenue before the reduction of vouchers and adjusted for certain IFRS reclassification effects. The audited IFRS "Revenue" line in the Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss is €12,294.7m for FY2024 (vouchers of −€884.1m and other reconciliation effects of +€382.4m bridge the two) [FY24 AR, p.108, "Reconciliation Total Segment Revenue to Revenue"]. This IFRS revenue figure is disclosed only at Group level, not broken out by segment.

## 2. Dominant Segment

**MENA is the dominant segment on profit — the metric that matters — even though Asia is larger on revenue.** MENA generated €472.9m of Adjusted EBITDA in FY2024, 68.3% of the Group's €692.5m total and the single largest segment contributor, at the best margin of any segment (13.4% Adj. EBITDA/segment revenue, up from 11.3% in 2023) [FY24 AR, "Key Figures" p.4]. Asia is larger by revenue (31.8% vs. MENA's 27.6% of Total Segment Revenue) but contributes less profit (55.6% vs. 68.3%) at a lower and flatter margin (9.5%, roughly unchanged from 10.3% in 2023) because of the competitive pressure described above [FY24 AR, p.4, p.105]. Per this module's rule, when revenue and profit shares disagree, the dominant segment is named by profit: **MENA**.

MENA does not clear the 85% threshold for "effectively single-segment" (it is 68.3% of profit and 27.6% of revenue), so Delivery Hero remains a genuinely multi-segment business — the other four segments together still generate 31.7% of Group Adj. EBITDA (and Asia alone is 55.6%, a large second contributor), and two segments (Europe, Integrated Verticals) are net drags on Group profit.

**FY2025 directional cross-check (unaudited, Tier 5/6 — not the primary basis for this finding):** per a Capital IQ workbook export tied to the Mar-26-2026 FY2025 earnings call, MENA's dominance appears to have widened in FY2025 — segment Adj. EBITDA of €546.0m (60.5% of the €902.8m segment-level sum) vs. Asia's €333.1m (36.9%), with Asia's Adj. EBITDA actually declining year-over-year [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab, Dec-31-2025 column]. This is consistent with, but not proof beyond, the FY2024 audited finding above; no audited FY2025 segment note is present in this pool to confirm it at Tier-1 quality.

## 3. Segment Disclosure Quality

Segment definitions are broadly consistent year-over-year — the same five segments (Asia, MENA, Europe, Americas, Integrated Verticals) appear across FY2020–FY2024 in both the Annual Report and the Capital IQ financials export — but the underlying historical figures have been restated or reclassified repeatedly: the Capital IQ segment history is labeled "Restated" for FY2020–FY2022 and "Reclassified" for FY2023, meaning the segment revenue/Adj. EBITDA figures reported for a given historical year have changed across successive annual filings [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab, column headers]. There is no discrete "Other" or "Corporate" segment row in the reportable-segment table itself, but a large centralized reconciling bucket sits between segment profit and Group statutory profit: "Unallocated Management Adjustments" (−€511.9m in FY2024) plus "Unallocated Expenses for Share-Based Compensation" (−€171.1m in FY2024) total −€683.0m — almost exactly offsetting the €692.5m of segment-level Adjusted EBITDA — which is why the Group's audited IFRS operating result was actually a loss of −€341.3m and net result a loss of −€881.7m in FY2024, despite segment Adjusted EBITDA showing a €692.5m profit [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab; FY24 AR, p.107, "Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss"]. This is the single biggest disclosure-quality issue: **profit is disclosed at segment level only on a heavily adjusted, non-IFRS basis** (Adjusted EBITDA is defined by management to exclude share-based compensation, legal/antitrust and courier-reclassification expenses, restructuring costs, corporate-transaction costs, and IFRS 16 right-of-use depreciation [FY24 AR, p.101, footnote 5]), and the bridge back to audited IFRS profit is a large, unallocated, Group-level item that the segment table gives no way to attribute to any one segment. A second disclosure gap specific to MENA: the segment consolidates 100% of talabat's results even though DH holds only an 80% economic interest following talabat's December 2024 Dubai listing, so the segment table alone cannot be used to size DHER shareholders' actual claim on MENA profit without a further minority-interest adjustment [FY24 AR, p.106]. No FY2025 audited annual report or segment note is present in this pool; FY2025 segment figures used above are sourced only from a Capital IQ workbook export tied to a Mar-26-2026 earnings-call transcript (Tier 5/6), not an audited filing.

## 4. Citations

- GMV segment-share pie chart (48% Asia / 26% MENA / 18% Europe / 8% Americas): `FY24 Annual Report, "Delivery Hero Worldwide", p.4–5`
- Segment definitions, business model, brands, and country lists per segment: `FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, A. Group Profile §3 "Segments", p.100–101`
- Adjusted EBITDA definition (non-IFRS, exclusions listed): `FY24 Annual Report, p.101, footnote 5`
- Total Segment Revenue definition and reconciliation to IFRS Revenue (€12,796.4m → €12,294.7m): `FY24 Annual Report, B.2 "Business Performance" / "Reconciliation Total Segment Revenue to Revenue", p.108`
- 2024 targets-and-results table, Asia competition commentary, Europe/Italy rider-reclassification driver of the EBITDA miss, MENA/Americas commentary, talabat 20% listing / 80% retained stake: `FY24 Annual Report, B.2 "Business Performance", p.105–106`

## business-model / 04_unit-economics.md

_Source: `business-model/04_unit-economics.md`_

# Unit Economics — DHER

Basis: Delivery Hero SE (XTRA:DHER), Prime Standard / Frankfurt Stock Exchange, IFRS as adopted by the EU, EUR, fiscal year ending Dec-31. Figures below are FY2024 (year ended Dec-31-2024) from the audited FY2024 Annual Report (published Apr 25, 2025) unless stated otherwise. FY2025 figures are explicitly labeled Capital IQ workbook / earnings-transcript sourced (Tier 5/6, per `analyses/DHER_2026-08-12/business-model/00_data-triage.md`) — no audited FY2025 annual report or `ciq_facts.json` sidecar exists in this pool.

Upstream input used: `03_segment-map.md` (present) identifies **MENA** as the dominant segment on profit — 68.3% of Group Adjusted EBITDA (€472.9m of €692.5m) at the best segment margin (13.4% Adj. EBITDA/Segment Revenue, up from 11.3%), even though Asia is larger by revenue [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures" p.4]. This report builds the unit-economics table for MENA.

## 1. Natural Unit

The natural economic unit for MENA is **the order** — a single food-delivery or quick-commerce transaction placed through a MENA platform brand (talabat, Hungerstation, InstaShop, or Yemeksepeti) [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, A.3 "Segments", p.100–101]. Delivery Hero itself frames its economics this way: "GMV is influenced by the number of orders, as well as average basket size per order" [FY24 Annual Report, p.5081-region text].

A second, structurally different unit exists in the Integrated Verticals segment: the **Dmart (quick-commerce) order**, where Delivery Hero acts as principal — buying and reselling inventory through its own warehouses rather than earning a commission — giving that unit a merchandise-margin economic structure instead of MENA's commission-based one [FY24 Annual Report, p.101].

## 2. Unit Economics Table

**Caveat before the table: Delivery Hero does not disclose an absolute order count, an average order value in currency, or a segment-level customer-acquisition cost anywhere in the pool — for MENA or for the Group.** The only segment-level per-volume metric it discloses is Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of GMV (a monetary-basket proxy, not a literal per-order figure). Most rows below are therefore "Not disclosed" at the true unit level; where a Group-level or GMV-normalized proxy exists, it is shown and labeled as a proxy, not as the per-order number the row asks for.

| Unit Economic | Value | Period | Direction vs Prior Year (Improving / Stable / Deteriorating / Unknown) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue per unit | Not disclosed | — | Unknown | DHER discloses order growth only as a percentage at Group level (e.g., "acceleration of order growth to 10%, up from 9% in Q4" — Group, not MENA) and GMV/Segment Revenue in euros by segment, but never publishes an absolute order count or average order value for MENA or the Group, so revenue-per-order cannot be computed from filings [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures" p.4; Q1 2026 Sales/Trading Statement Call transcript, p.6 — Tier 6] |
| Gross margin per unit | Not disclosed at segment level | FY2024 | Unknown | Only a Group-level "gross profit to GMV" ratio is disclosed: 6.8% in 2024 vs 6.6% in 2023 (+0.2 percentage points, pp), alongside Group gross profit margin (gross profit / revenue) falling 2.8pp to 27.1% (2023: 29.9%) on rising own-delivery and Integrated Verticals mix — neither is broken out by segment, so MENA-specific gross margin per order cannot be isolated [FY24 Annual Report, B.3 "Results of Operations", p.108] |
| Contribution margin per unit (after variable costs) | MENA Adjusted EBITDA / GMV = 3.7% | FY2024 (vs. FY2023: 3.1%) | **Improving** (+0.6pp) | Closest disclosed proxy for MENA — Adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of segment GMV. This is not a strict contribution margin: Adjusted EBITDA already nets out delivery costs, marketing, IT and G&A (management-defined, excludes share-based compensation, legal/antitrust and rider-reclassification provisions, restructuring, and IFRS 16 depreciation), not only variable costs [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures" p.4; p.101, footnote 5]. FY2025 cross-check (Tier 5, Capital IQ workbook, unaudited): MENA Adj. EBITDA / Segment Revenue was ~13.5% (€546.0m / €4,033.7m) vs. 13.4% in FY2024 — essentially flat, not a further step-change gain [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab, Dec-31-2025 column] |
| Cost to acquire / build the unit | Not disclosed at segment or per-order level | FY2024 Group total: €484.8m ("Customer acquisition" line within Marketing Expenses), down 2.9% from €499.3m in FY2023 | Unknown at unit level; Group aggregate **improving** (falling in absolute terms while volume grew) | The Group "Customer acquisition" cost line — TV/radio/offline marketing €200.3m, search engine marketing (SEM)/search engine optimization (SEO) €97.7m, other (social media, display, mobile) €186.8m, totaling €484.8m — is disclosed only at Group level, with no MENA-specific split and no accompanying new-customer count or cost-per-order figure [FY24 Annual Report, Consolidated Financial Statements, Note G.3 "Marketing Expenses", p.~9405] |
| Payback period or unit lifetime | Not disclosed numerically | — | Unknown | Management describes the economics only in qualitative terms: customer acquisition "has a very long payback period, but a very high payback [return]," contrasted with voucher-driven order boosts that have "a very immediate impact" — no month/year figure, cohort table, or LTV:CAC ratio is given [Q1 2026 Sales/Trading Statement Call transcript, Q&A — Tier 6, not from filings] |

## 3. Value Creation Read

**Unclear at the true per-order level — but the one disclosed proxy points toward value creation, not destruction.** MENA's Adjusted EBITDA / GMV margin rose from 3.1% to 3.7% in FY2024 while segment GMV grew +28.8% [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures" p.4] — the only segment combining double-digit volume growth with an already meaningfully positive relative margin (Asia's is 1.6%, and Europe/Integrated Verticals are negative). That is consistent with each incremental order adding profit rather than diluting it. But Delivery Hero discloses no order count, no average order value, and no acquisition cost tied to a single order or a single new customer for MENA (or the Group), so the contribution-margin-×-lifetime-vs-acquisition-cost math this section is meant to test cannot actually be built from filings — only inferred from a GMV-normalized EBITDA margin, which is a coarser proxy. **The single most valuable missing disclosure is MENA-segment (or even Group-level) absolute order count and average order value**, which would let revenue-per-order and a real per-order contribution margin be computed directly instead of inferred.

**Peak-cycle ring-fence:** FY2024's MENA acceleration (+28.8% GMV, +55.3% Adj. EBITDA, margin +0.6pp) coincided with talabat's Dec-2024 Dubai Financial Market listing and management's own comment that MENA "performed significantly better than expected" [FY24 Annual Report, p.4]. The FY2025 cross-check (Tier 5, unaudited, Capital IQ workbook) shows MENA revenue growth decelerating sharply to +14.3% (€3,527.8m → €4,033.7m) while the Adj. EBITDA/revenue margin only held flat (13.4% → ~13.5%), not expanding further [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab]. Read the 3.1%→3.7% GMV-margin improvement as a strong-year result that stabilized rather than compounded further in FY2025 — not yet proven as a structurally rising margin.

## 4. Sensitivity

The single input most likely to swing this read if it moved 20% is **delivery cost per order** (the largest and most volatile cost-of-sales line). Group delivery expenses grew 33.9% in FY2024 (€4,496.0m → €6,022.1m) — faster than the 23.7% growth in Group revenue — and management attributed part of the excess directly to "intensified competition in certain regions, which led to increased logistic expenses" [FY24 Annual Report, B.3 "Results of Operations", p.106]. Delivery expenses represent 67.2% of Group cost of sales (2023: 64.5%) [FY24 Annual Report, p.106], so a 20% adverse move in per-order delivery cost — the same dynamic already visible in Asia, where GMV fell −7.7% under competitive pressure and margin stayed flat despite revenue growth [FY24 Annual Report, p.105–106] — would compress MENA's 3.7% Adj. EBITDA/GMV margin far more than an equivalent move in marketing spend (€484.8m, already falling) or IT costs (1.1% of GMV). A second, structural sensitivity specific to MENA: the segment table consolidates 100% of talabat's results even though DH holds only an 80% economic interest post-listing [FY24 Annual Report, p.106] — so roughly a fifth of any MENA per-unit profit improvement accrues to talabat's public minority shareholders, not to DHER shareholders directly, which the GMV-margin proxy above does not adjust for.

## business-model / 05_customer-geography.md

_Source: `business-model/05_customer-geography.md`_

# Customer And Geography Map — DHER

## 1. Customer Map

Delivery Hero does not disclose any single named customer or counterparty (expected for a consumer marketplace — its revenue is earned from millions of individual consumer orders and roughly 500,000+ restaurant/vendor partners, none of which could plausibly reach a disclosure threshold). The company instead discloses revenue by **nature/fee type** in its audited revenue note, which is the closest available proxy for "who pays." Figures below are FY2024 (year ended Dec-31-2024), the latest audited period.

| Customer Type | Importance (% of revenue if disclosed) | Long-term Contract? (Y/N/Not disclosed) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Restaurant / vendor partners — commission fees (platform take-rate on orders) | €5,092.6m / €12,294.7m total revenue = 41.4% | Not disclosed. Marketplace listing agreements are standard commission contracts; the filing does not disclose fixed terms or lock-in periods. Inference, not from filings: these read as at-will, cancellable partner agreements typical of food-delivery marketplaces, not multi-year supply contracts. | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1 (Disaggregation of Revenue by Nature), p.181 | Fragmented across a large, undisclosed number of restaurant partners — no single vendor named or sized. Regulatory/competition risk (EU antitrust investigation, provisioned at €225.5m in FY24 G&A) could compress this take-rate. |
| Restaurant / vendor partners — advertising and listing fees (AdTech, premium placement) | €1,438.3m / €12,294.7m = 11.7% | Not disclosed | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 | Same fragmented-partner base as commission fees; a discretionary marketing spend that vendors can cut first in a downturn. |
| Consumers — delivery fees (charged separately for delivery service) | €2,966.0m / €12,294.7m = 24.1% | N — pay-per-order, no contract | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 | Diffuse consumer base; price-sensitive to competitor promotions and voucher intensity (vouchers reduced FY24 revenue by €884.1m). |
| Consumers — subscription fees (DH+ / loyalty programs) plus service fees | €322.8m + €139.6m = €462.4m / €12,294.7m = 3.8% | N — cancellable subscriptions | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 | Small, growing (+63.1% service fees, +52.8% subscription fees YoY) but still a minor share; not a locked-in recurring base. |
| Direct retail customers — Integrated Verticals / "Dmarts" (quick-commerce, DH sells groceries and goods directly) | €2,445.3m / €12,294.7m = 19.9% | N — one-off retail purchases | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 | This is the one segment where DH is the seller of record, not just the platform — inventory and demand risk sit with DH directly (Dmarts cost of sales €1,992.9m, FY24 Annual Report Note G.3). |
| Payment fees / other | €559.7m + €214.6m = €774.3m / €12,294.7m = 6.3% | N | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 | Minor, ancillary. |

Note: percentages sum to slightly above 100% before the €884.1m voucher deduction is netted against the gross fee lines; the table shows the gross composition the company discloses, consistent with Note G.1's own presentation.

**Intercompany "customer" data note:** the Capital IQ customer export in this pool (`Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Customers.rtf`) lists entities such as Talabat Holding, Glovoapp23, and a household-products borrower as "customers" — on inspection these are borrower/intercompany relationships tied to Delivery Hero's own M&A and financing structure (e.g., Talabat and Glovoapp23 are DH's own majority-owned subsidiaries), not third-party revenue customers. This is not usable for revenue-concentration purposes and is excluded from the table above.

## 2. Geography Map

Delivery Hero discloses geography two ways in its audited filing: (a) an operating-segment view by region (Asia, MENA, Europe, Americas, Integrated Verticals), and (b) an IFRS 8 geographic note by individual country where revenue is "material" (Korea, UAE, Saudi Arabia, all other countries pooled). The country-level note is used below because it is the actual consolidated-revenue geographic disclosure and reconciles to total revenue; the regional/segment view is shown for context in the Evidence column.

| Geography | % of Revenue | Trend (Growing / Stable / Declining / Unknown) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| South Korea | FY2024: 23.8% (€2,926.1m / €12,294.7m); FY2025: 23.4% (€3,285.9m / €14,059.6m, transcript/CIQ-sourced) | Stable to slightly declining as a share, though absolute revenue still growing | FY24 Annual Report, Note (Geographic Segments) via Capital IQ Financials workbook, Segments tab [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments]; company text: "Our largest market, South Korea..." [FY24 Annual Report, Economic Report, p.~103] | Explicitly named by the company as its single largest country market. Korean-won FX exposure and Korea-specific competitive/regulatory dynamics (e.g. Baemin discount events, antitrust scrutiny of Korean delivery platforms) concentrate risk in one jurisdiction. |
| Saudi Arabia | FY2024: 8.6% (€1,056.1m); FY2025: 7.6% (€1,065.4m) | Declining as a share | Same source | Company calls Saudi Arabia "our largest market in the region" (MENA) [FY24 Annual Report, Economic Report, p.~104]. Regional geopolitical/oil-cycle sensitivity. |
| United Arab Emirates | FY2024: 8.3% (€1,014.8m); FY2025: 8.9% (€1,254.6m) | Growing as a share | Same source | Second-largest single-country disclosure in MENA; regional geopolitical exposure. |
| All other countries (pooled, not individually broken out — spans Asia ex-Korea, MENA ex-Saudi/UAE, Europe, Americas) | FY2024: 59.4% (€7,297.7m); FY2025: 60.1% (€8,453.7m) | Growing as a share (diversifying) | Same source | Opaque at country level — the company does not disclose which countries within this "Other" bucket are individually material, so true single-country concentration inside this bucket cannot be assessed from available data. Not proven from available data. |

**Regional operating-segment view (context, FY2024, share of Group GMV, sums to 100%):** Asia 48%, MENA 26%, Europe 18%, Americas 8% [FY24 Annual Report, "Delivery Hero Worldwide," p.5]. This is a GMV (order-value) share, not a revenue share — GMV is the value of goods/services transacted on the platform, most of which is passed through to restaurants and riders, not booked as DH revenue. The Asia segment's dominance here is driven overwhelmingly by South Korea (Woowa/Baemin).

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | N — not disclosed / not applicable. No single restaurant, vendor, or consumer counterparty is disclosed or plausible at this scale; revenue is disaggregated by fee TYPE, not by named customer, and each type spans millions of orders / hundreds of thousands of partners. | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | N — same reasoning; not a named-customer business | FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181 |
| One geography >50% of revenue | N — largest single disclosed country (South Korea) is 23.8% of FY2024 revenue. The 59.4% "Other Countries" bucket is an aggregate of many jurisdictions, not one geography, so it does not trigger this flag on its own, though it does mean a large share of revenue is not disclosed at single-country granularity. | FY24 Annual Report, Segments note [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab] |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | N on the strict >30% threshold (Korea is 23.8%, below 30%), but flagged as a near-miss: Korea is the company's own named "largest market," commission/delivery relationships there are not disclosed as long-term contracts (Inference, not from filings), and Korea revenue is exposed to Korean-won FX and Korea-specific competitive/regulatory dynamics without any contractual protection. | FY24 Annual Report, Economic Report, p.~103; Note G.1, p.181 |

## 4. Read

This is a geography-concentrated business, not a customer-concentrated one: the customer side is inherently diffuse (millions of consumer orders, hundreds of thousands of restaurant/vendor partners, no named counterparty anywhere near a disclosure threshold), but South Korea alone supplies 23.8% of FY2024 revenue and is explicitly named by the company as its "largest market" [FY24 Annual Report, Economic Report, p.~103], with the broader Asia region (48% of Group GMV) dominated by that one country. None of this concentration is contractually secured — Korean consumers and restaurant partners transact on a pay-per-order, at-will basis with no long-term contract disclosed (Inference, not from filings), so the revenue is naked to Korean-won FX moves, local competitive intensity (e.g., discount events, subscription rebuilds discussed on the FY2025 earnings call), and Korea-specific regulatory action. The single biggest dependency the synthesizer should know about: roughly a quarter of Group revenue rests on one country (South Korea) that the company itself calls its largest market, with no long-term contract or hedge disclosed against that exposure.

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — DHER

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platform / Marketplace (commission model — restaurant & shop delivery) | Delivery Hero lists restaurants and shops on local-brand apps (talabat, Baemin, foodpanda, PedidosYa, Glovo/foodora/efood) and takes "a contractually specified percentage of the order amount" without ever owning the food or goods sold [FY24 Annual Report, p.100]. | Mid | Mid | Upstream: commission terms are set by DH contract, but restaurant supply is fragmented, DH spent €641.3m on "restaurant acquisition" marketing in FY2024 (2023: €626.5m) to keep winning listings, and regulators explicitly flag "commission caps" as a live legal risk that would remove DH's rate-setting power [FY24 Annual Report, p.109, p.128]. Downstream: subscription (up to 61% of GMV in Saudi Arabia) and multi-vertical bundling raise switching costs, but the Asia segment's GMV fell 7.7% in FY2024 "mainly driven by rising competition in certain regions" — proof that consumers do switch when a rival undercuts [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.105–106; Q1 2026 Trading Statement Call]. |
| Service provider (last-mile logistics — "own delivery") | DH is increasingly the delivery fleet itself rather than leaving delivery to the restaurant or a third party: own-delivery reached 78% of group orders in FY2025 (up from 67% in FY2024), letting DH capture the delivery fee instead of leaving it with someone else [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks]. | Strong (today), High regulatory tail risk | Strong | Upstream (rider labor): delivery expenses of €6,022.2m in FY2024 are 93.7% external riders/third-party logistics (€5,644.3m) versus only 6.3% DH's own rider fleet (€377.9m) [FY24 Annual Report, p.109] — riders accept or reject each task after seeing the offered pay via DH's own algorithm, giving DH day-to-day price-setting power. But this is capped by "High"-rated regulatory risk: Italian courts confirmed rider reclassification in Apr-2025 (provision updated), Spain is moving Glovo to an employment model from Jul-2025, and the disclosed contingent liability for the Spanish courier-fleet reclassification alone is €440.0m–€770.0m [FY24 Annual Report, p.126–128, p.203–204]. Downstream: separately charged delivery fees grew 22.4% year-over-year with no disclosed volume pushback [FY24 Annual Report, p.108]. |
| Retailer / Principal (quick commerce — Dmarts) | DH buys and holds groceries, electronics and household items in its own warehouses (Dmarts, 48 countries) and sells them directly to the customer, recognizing close to the full retail price as revenue because it is the seller of record, not a commission agent [FY24 Annual Report, p.100–101]. | Not proven from available data | Weak | Upstream: no supplier concentration, sourcing-cost, or wholesale-terms disclosure exists in the pool for Dmarts inventory — "Not proven from available data." Downstream: the segment (Integrated Verticals) still posted a −3.6% Adjusted EBITDA/segment revenue margin in FY2024 (improved from −10.2% in 2023 but not yet breakeven), meaning the business cannot yet price to cover its own delivery-plus-goods cost in a competitive quick-commerce market — a price-taker state, not a price-setter one [Segment Map, §1; FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.106]. |
| Platform / Marketplace — advertising layer (AdTech) | DH sells in-app placement to restaurants and consumer-goods brands across both the marketplace and Dmarts businesses, a stream management describes as "approaching a EUR 1.5 billion revenue run rate," explicitly framed as "moving us beyond a reliance on commission alone" [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks]. | N/A — no material input cost disclosed for this stream | Strong (Inference, not from filings — no disclosed price resistance) | Advertising revenue is layered on top of an audience DH already owns; there is no comparable channel for a restaurant or CPG brand to reach the same in-app customer base disclosed in the pool. No advertiser-concentration or churn data is disclosed, so "Strong" downstream is an inference from the revenue growth and management framing, not a filing-quantified pricing metric. |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Delivery Hero's largest input cost — delivery expenses (external riders, third-party logistics, and DH's own rider fleet) — rose to 67.2% of total cost of sales in FY2024, up from 64.5% in FY2023, and cost of sales grew 28.6% year-over-year versus revenue growth of 23.7% [FY24 Annual Report, p.108–109]. The filing does not describe any contractual pass-through mechanism, escalator, or indexed-pricing clause tying commission or delivery-fee rates to rider cost inflation; instead, management's stated levers are mix shift (own-delivery capturing the fee itself) and operational efficiency ("order stacking levels" and logistics centralization "help to bring down the cost per order") [FY24 Annual Report, p.135]. Where a cost shock was regulatory rather than commercial, DH did not pass it through — it absorbed it: the Europe segment's FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA miss versus the Group's own 2024 target range (€692.5m actual vs. €725–775m guided) was specifically attributed to "additional expenses recognized for rider-related reclassification risks in Italy," and Europe's segment margin stayed negative (−4.1% Adjusted EBITDA/segment revenue) [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.106; Segment Map, §1]. The one demonstrated lever that functions like a price increase is discount reduction: vouchers fell from 8.1% to 6.9% of Total Segment Revenue in FY2024 while GMV still grew 7.7%, showing DH can pull back subsidies without an immediate, filing-visible volume loss at group level [FY24 Annual Report, p.109].

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The dominant, quantified input dependency is on external/freelance labor for delivery, not on a raw-material supplier: 93.7% of FY2024 delivery expense (€5,644.3m of €6,022.2m) went to external riders and third-party logistics providers rather than DH's own employed fleet (€377.9m, 6.3%) [FY24 Annual Report, p.109]. This is a material single-category dependency — the company runs its core last-mile function overwhelmingly through a workforce it does not directly employ, which is precisely the population subject to the reclassification risk described in §1 and §5. For the Dmarts principal business, no supplier concentration is disclosed: there is no figure in the pool for the largest goods supplier's share of Dmarts cost of sales, no single-source input identified, and no wholesale-terms disclosure — "Not proven from available data," and this is itself a disclosure gap rather than evidence of low concentration.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

The evidence is regionally split rather than uniform. In DH's strongest market, MENA (talabat), the company both raised its margin and pulled back discounting: MENA's Adjusted EBITDA/segment revenue rose to 13.4% in FY2024 from 11.3% in 2023, and management called the segment's performance "significantly better than expected" [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.105]. Loyalty tools reinforce this — subscription penetration reached up to 61% of GMV in Saudi Arabia by Q1 2026, and in Korea the newly relaunched subscription program is "nearly 50% of total order volumes" [Q1 2026 Trading Statement Call; FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, Q&A]. Set against that, the Asia segment's GMV fell 7.7% in FY2024 "mainly driven by rising competition in certain regions," and Adjusted EBITDA there stayed flat at a lower 9.5% margin despite 9.2% revenue growth — direct evidence that DH lost volume rather than holding price when a rival undercut it in a specific market [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.105–106]. No explicit list-price or commission-rate increase in the last 24 months is disclosed in the pool with an associated volume read; the only quantified pricing-adjacent action is the voucher pull-back described in §2, which management ties to "improved" margins without a stated volume cost.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.**

Delivery Hero sets price and captures rising margin in its dominant regional market (MENA, 13.4% Adjusted EBITDA/segment revenue and rising) and has built a fast-growing, apparently price-setting advertising layer (nearing a €1.5bn run rate) that management explicitly uses to reduce dependence on restaurant commissions [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.105; FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026]. But it is a price-taker in its second-largest segment by revenue (Asia, where GMV fell 7.7% on competition), in its fastest-growing new business line (Dmarts/quick commerce, still at a −3.6% segment margin), and — structurally — over the labor input that makes up two-thirds of its cost of sales, where 93.7% of delivery spend runs through external/freelance riders now facing an active, multi-jurisdiction reclassification threat [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, p.106, p.109, p.126–128].

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

Rider employment reclassification: with 93.7% of delivery expense running through external/freelance riders and a disclosed Spain contingent liability of €440.0m–€770.0m on top of an already-triggered Italy provision, a broader shift from freelance to employed rider status across the EU or Latin America would convert DH's largest, currently most controllable cost line into a much less flexible, regulator-set one [FY24 Annual Report, p.109, p.126–128, p.203–204].

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — DHER

Upstream inputs read: `02_business-identity.md`, `03_segment-map.md`, `05_customer-geography.md` — all present. No upstream gap to flag.

**Sector overlay (step 2b):** `02_business-identity.md` (§3a) classifies DHER as a two-sided food/quick-commerce marketplace converting part of itself into an owned-inventory retailer (Integrated Verticals / "Dmarts"), with no exact row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` for "on-demand delivery marketplace." The nearest analogue used there is the **Retail / consumer** row. *Sector overlay applied: Retail / consumer (nearest analogue, no exact marketplace row exists) — capital intensity, margin stability and cyclicality below use the retail lens (like-for-like GMV growth as the SSSG-equivalent, gross-margin/inventory read for the Dmarts principal leg); pricing power and competitive intensity are read through the two-sided-marketplace take-rate lens instead, since the retail overlay has no KPI for a commission-based agent model.* This is a hybrid application, not a clean single-sector fit — flagged explicitly per the instruction not to skip step 2b silently.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 32 | Gross profit-to-GMV ratio (the Group's effective blended take rate) was just 6.8% in FY2024, up only 0.2 points from 6.6% in FY2023 [FY24 Annual Report, p.108]. Commission is "a contractually specified percentage of the order amount" that "varies by country, restaurant type" [FY24 Annual Report, p.100] — i.e. set market-by-market, not a group-wide lever. Management is building AdTech (~€1.5bn revenue run rate) explicitly to reduce "reliance on commission alone" [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks] | A thin, competitively-capped take rate that the company itself is trying to supplement rather than raise — weak pricing power on the core transaction. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 40 | Every order is a discrete, pay-per-order transaction with no long-term contract disclosed on either the restaurant or the consumer side (Inference, not from filings) [FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181]. Subscription revenue (DH+) is only 3.8% of total revenue (€322.8m of €12,294.7m) though growing +52.8% YoY [FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181]. "Enhanced customer experience and boosted order frequency" is cited as a driver [FY24 Annual Report, p.108] but this is habitual re-ordering, not contracted recurrence. | Mostly one-off transactions; a small, fast-growing subscription layer is the only genuinely recurring piece. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 30 | Marketing expenses were €1,450.8m in FY2024 (3.0% of GMV), including €641.3m of restaurant acquisition spend and €484.8m of customer acquisition spend [FY24 Annual Report, p.108] — continuous spend is required just to hold position. Asia segment GMV fell −7.7% in FY2024 "mainly driven by rising competition in certain regions" [FY24 Annual Report, p.105] — direct evidence customers switch when a rival undercuts. | Multi-homing is the norm in food delivery; the company has to keep buying loyalty with vouchers and acquisition spend rather than earning it structurally. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 28 | Gross margin fell from 29.9% (FY2023) to 27.1% (FY2024) to 24.4% (FY2025, CIQ) as own-delivery and Integrated Verticals mix rose [FY24 Annual Report, p.108; Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Income Statement tab]. Group operating income was negative every year FY2020–FY2024 and only turned marginally positive in FY2025 (€93.7m, 0.7% of revenue) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Income Statement tab]. The FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA of €692.5m missed the company's own €725–775m guided range because of added provisions "for rider-related reclassification risks in Italy" [FY24 Annual Report, p.9, p.105–106]. | Margins move with regulatory provisions, mix shift and competitive intensity, not with a stable underlying structure — this is the single most exposed row on this table. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 76 | Capex was €139.1m in FY2024 (1.1% of revenue) and €171.0m in FY2025 (1.2% of revenue), down from €267.1m (4.6% of revenue) in FY2021 [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab]. The core marketplace model is agent-based (no inventory, no owned assets) [FY24 Annual Report, p.100]; Dmarts warehouses add some asset intensity but are not separately capitalized in the filing (Inference, not from filings). | Genuinely capital-light at the group level — the strongest row on this table. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 16 | The pool's competitor list names dozens of well-funded rivals across every geography — Uber Eats/DoorDash (which now owns Deliveroo), Grab, Swiggy/Eternal (Blinkit/Zomato), GoPuff, Getir, JOKR, Careem, Jahez, Prosus/Just Eat Takeaway, and local champions like Talabat's own regional rivals — all competing directly with DHER's brands (talabat, foodpanda, Glovo, PedidosYa, Baemin) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Competitors.rtf/.txt]. Asia GMV fell outright (−7.7%) in FY2024 on "rising competition" [FY24 Annual Report, p.105]. Quick commerce specifically has seen "multiple competitor failures/consolidations industry-wide" [`02_business-identity.md`, §3a]. | One of the most crowded competitive fields in consumer tech — global platforms, regional champions, and adjacent super-apps all fighting for the same orders. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 26 | DHER's own business model is still shifting under it: own-delivery share of orders rose from 67% to 78% in a single year, and Integrated Verticals (the principal/inventory model) grew GMV over 30% YoY [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks]. The sub-sector has already seen repeated competitor failures and consolidation (DoorDash–Deliveroo, Prosus–Just Eat Takeaway), rider-employment rules are actively being rewritten market by market (Spain, Italy) [FY24 Annual Report, p.8–9, p.105–106], and DHER itself is now the subject of a live Uber acquisition offer announced mid-2026 [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. | The winners in on-demand delivery/quick commerce are still being sorted by M&A and regulation in real time — this is not a settled industry. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 27 | An EU Commission antitrust investigation into alleged violations led DHER to increase a legal provision "to further ensure its financial stability" [FY24 Annual Report, p.9] — a related G&A provision of €225.5m is disclosed for FY2024 [`05_customer-geography.md`, citing FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181]. Rider-classification law changes directly cost money and forced a business-model change (Glovo moving to an employment-based rider model in Spain in 2025) [FY24 Annual Report, p.8–9]. Italy rider-reclassification provisions were the stated reason the Group missed its own FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA guidance [FY24 Annual Report, p.9, p.105–106]. | Regulation (antitrust, gig-worker classification) is already moving the P&L, not a hypothetical risk. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 66 | The marketplace/agent segments carry no direct commodity exposure — DHER does not buy or hold the food being delivered [FY24 Annual Report, p.100]. The Integrated Verticals/Dmarts leg does hold grocery/FMCG inventory, so food and household-goods input prices pass through Cost of Goods Sold there, but this is disclosed only at the blended Group Cost of Goods Sold line (€8,965.5m FY2024), not decomposed by commodity [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Income Statement tab]. Fuel/vehicle costs are borne mostly by third-party/self-employed riders, not DHER directly (Inference, not from filings). | Mostly a labor- and marketing-cost business, not a raw-material one — the one clean secondary strength alongside capital intensity. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 42 | Consumer discretionary spend exposure; Argentina and Türkiye results carry IAS 29 hyperinflation adjustments that distort comparability [`03_segment-map.md`, citing FY24 Annual Report, p.4 footnote, p.106]. Management flagged "USD and Korean won devaluation" as an active FY2026 headwind [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks]. Asia GMV declined in FY2024 even in a still-growing overall market, showing demand is not insulated from local macro/competitive swings [FY24 Annual Report, p.105]. | Moderate — not a classic commodity-cycle business, but FX, hyperinflation accounting, and discretionary-spend sensitivity all move results meaningfully year to year. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 46 | The company publishes a full audited annual report with a revenue-by-nature note (Note G.1) and a geographic note, and reconciles Total Segment Revenue to IFRS Revenue explicitly (€12,796.4m → €12,294.7m) [FY24 Annual Report, p.108]. But segment-level profit is disclosed only on a heavily adjusted, non-IFRS Adjusted EBITDA basis, with a €683.0m unallocated bridge (Unallocated Management Adjustments + Unallocated SBC) between segment Adj. EBITDA (€692.5m) and the audited Group operating result (−€341.3m) that cannot be attributed to any one segment [`03_segment-map.md`, citing FY24 Annual Report, p.107, Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls]. The MENA segment table consolidates 100% of talabat's result despite DHER holding only an 80% economic interest post-listing, without a segment-level minority adjustment [`03_segment-map.md`, citing FY24 Annual Report, p.106]. Historical segment figures are also labeled "Restated"/"Reclassified" across multiple vintages [`03_segment-map.md`, citing Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab]. | Extensive in volume, but the profit bridge is opaque enough that a reader cannot reconstruct true segment-level IFRS profitability from the disclosure alone. |

Bands: 0–20 Very weak · 21–40 Weak · 41–60 Mixed/Average · 61–80 Strong · 81–100 Very strong.

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 34/100 (Weak).**

**Band-anchor check:** row scores sorted ascending are 16, 26, 27, 28, 30, 32, 40, 42, 46, 66, 76. The second-lowest row is 26 (industry rate-of-change), so the aggregate may not exceed 26 + 20 = 46. The aggregate of 34 sits within that ceiling.

Weighting: the read is dominated by three factors that define whether this is a survivable, ownable business — **margin stability (28), competitive intensity (16), and industry rate-of-change (26)** — because a marketplace that cannot hold a stable margin in a still-consolidating, still-regulating industry cannot be underwritten as a durable compounder regardless of how light its balance sheet is. These three get roughly 55% of the weight. **Pricing power (32), customer stickiness (30) and regulatory dependence (27)** get secondary weight (~30% combined) — they reinforce the same story (thin, contested take rate; loyalty bought with vouchers; regulation already moving the P&L) rather than adding new information. **Capital intensity (76) and commodity dependence (66)** — the two genuinely strong rows — get the remaining ~15%: they matter (an asset-light, non-commodity cost structure is real) but cannot offset a business that is structurally low-margin and hyper-competitive.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Capital intensity | 76 | Capex has fallen to ~1.1–1.2% of revenue in FY2024–FY2025 on a fundamentally agent-based, no-inventory core marketplace model [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab; FY24 Annual Report, p.100]. |
| Weakest | Competitive intensity | 16 | Every regional brand DHER runs faces a well-funded direct rival (Uber Eats/DoorDash-Deliveroo, Grab, Swiggy/Eternal, GoPuff, Getir, JOKR, Jahez, Careem, Just Eat Takeaway/Prosus), and Asia GMV fell outright in FY2024 on rising competition [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Competitors.rtf/.txt; FY24 Annual Report, p.105]. |

## 4. Read

This is a hyper-competitive, capital-light, low-and-unstable-margin marketplace that is mid-transition from a pure commission agent into a part-owned-inventory quick-commerce retailer — closer to a sector/technology-cycle bet than a durable compounder. FY2025's first-ever Group operating profit (€93.7m, a 0.7% margin, up from years of losses) is not a cyclical peak to anchor against — it is a fragile, recent inflection funded by continued heavy marketing spend (3.0% of GMV) and still sitting on a gross margin that fell from 29.9% to 24.4% over two years [FY24 Annual Report, p.108; Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Income Statement tab] — the trend line matters more than the single positive quarter. The industry rate-of-change / disruption row scored 26 (≤40), so per CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 5 this thesis is flagged as a sector / technology-cycle bet rather than a durable compounder — reinforced by the fact that DHER itself is currently the subject of a live Uber acquisition offer (M&A call, Jul 16, 2026; expected close H2 2027) rather than being valued as a standalone, steady-state business [`02_business-identity.md`, §4, citing Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. The single factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is **margin stability**: whether the FY2025 inflection to positive operating income holds as own-delivery/Integrated Verticals mix keeps rising, competitive intensity in Asia persists, and rider-classification and EU antitrust costs continue to surface.

RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — DHER

Upstream dependencies confirmed present: `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md` both exist in this run folder and are used below. No missing-upstream caveat applies.

## 1. Dominant Segment

MENA is Delivery Hero's dominant segment by profit — 68.3% of FY2024 Group Adjusted EBITDA (€472.9m of €692.5m) at the best segment margin in the group (13.4% Adjusted EBITDA/segment revenue) — even though Asia is larger by revenue [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures" p.4; `03_segment-map.md`, Section 2]. The MENA segment is run almost entirely through talabat (80%-owned by Delivery Hero since its Dec-2024 Dubai listing) [FY24 Annual Report, p.4, footnote].

## 2. Named Competitors

### Competitor A — Uber Technologies, Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** NYSE:UBER
- **Where they compete:** Global — Uber Eats competes with foodpanda (Asia), Glovo/foodora/efood (Europe) and PedidosYa (Americas). In the Middle East specifically — Delivery Hero's dominant segment — Uber's own CEO directly compared Uber's Middle East delivery-and-mobility business to talabat: "when you look in the Middle East and compare Uber and talabat, both last year grew about 30% in terms of gross bookings ... They have a very large kind of consumer ecosystem and ... both have 8 million monthly active users. And then both have about really attractive margins as well, about 7% EBITDA margins as well. That is both businesses on a stand-alone basis." [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026, Dara Khosrowshahi (CEO) remarks]. Uber Technologies has also agreed to acquire all of Delivery Hero SE, expected to close H2 2027 — Uber is simultaneously DHER's largest global competitor and its pending acquirer [same source].
- **Scale:** FY2025 total revenue $52.017bn (Mobility + Delivery + Freight, company-wide) [Uber Technologies Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 4, 2026 (web, dated)]. Converted at the FY2025 average EUR/USD rate of 1.1306, Delivery Hero's FY2025 revenue of €14,059.8m is approximately $15.9bn [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab; FX: 2025 average EUR/USD 1.1306, X-Rates.com, accessed 2026-08-12] — Uber is roughly 3.3x DHER's scale group-wide.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 GAAP operating margin 10.7% ($5.565bn operating income / $52.017bn revenue); GAAP net margin 19.3% ($10.053bn net income / $52.017bn revenue) — the net margin is materially inflated by a one-off item (a large deferred-tax benefit disclosed in Uber's FY2025 results) and should not be read as a clean operating comparison; return on equity ~35.8% ($10.053bn net income / $28.083bn total stockholders' equity, Dec-31-2025), same one-off caveat applies; Adjusted EBITDA margin 4.5% of Gross Bookings ($8.730bn / $193.454bn) [Uber Technologies Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 4, 2026 (web, dated); balance-sheet figure per Uber FY2025 10-K, cited via SEC EDGAR filing index (web, dated)]. Segment-comparable to DHER's dominant segment: Uber's own Middle East delivery-and-mobility business runs at "about 7% EBITDA margins," which the CEO placed side-by-side with talabat's own ~7% margin in the same remark — both are described on a "stand-alone basis," i.e. before the deal's synergies [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. This is lower than the 13.4% Adjusted EBITDA/segment-revenue margin DHER discloses for its full MENA segment [FY24 Annual Report, p.4] — the two metrics are not on an identical basis (Uber's figure covers mobility+delivery combined; DHER's covers the marketplace-plus-Dmarts MENA segment), so the gap is directional evidence, not a clean like-for-like.
- **Source named in:** S&P Capital IQ Competitors export (Uber Technologies, Inc. matched against Delivery Hero SE (XTRA:DHER), sourced to DoorDash, Inc.'s 2024 Form 10-K) [`Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Competitors.rtf`]; directly and repeatedly in Uber's own M&A call announcing the acquisition of DHER [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026].
- **One-line read:** The company that most directly mirrors talabat's own growth rate, user base and margin in the Middle East is about to become DHER's owner — competitive rivalry and consolidation are the same event here.

### Competitor B — DoorDash, Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** NasdaqGS:DASH
- **Where they compete:** DoorDash acquired Deliveroo plc (closed Oct 2, 2025) and Wolt (2022), giving it direct delivery operations in the UK, Ireland, France, Italy, Belgium, Hong Kong, Singapore, and — via Deliveroo's Gulf footprint — the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar, putting it head-to-head with both DHER's Europe segment and, in the Gulf, with talabat in DHER's dominant MENA segment [Company Comparable Analysis, Business Description tab: "As of October 2, 2025, Deliveroo plc operates as a subsidiary of DoorDash, Inc."; countries per Deliveroo's own description in the same source].
- **Scale:** FY2025 total revenue $13.717bn [DoorDash Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 18, 2026 (web, dated)] versus DHER's FY2025 revenue of approximately $15.9bn (€14,059.8m at the 2025 average EUR/USD rate of 1.1306) — DoorDash is roughly 0.86x DHER's scale, comfortably inside the ~5x comparable-scale bound [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab; FX: X-Rates.com, accessed 2026-08-12].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 GAAP operating margin 5.3% ($723m operating income / $13.717bn revenue); GAAP net margin 6.8% ($935m net income attributable to DoorDash common stockholders / $13.717bn revenue) — DoorDash's first full year of GAAP profitability; return on equity approximately 9.3% ($935m net income / $10.033bn total stockholders' equity, Dec-31-2025) [DoorDash Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 18, 2026 (web, dated); balance sheet per DoorDash FY2025 10-K, cited via SEC EDGAR (web, dated)]. By contrast, DHER's audited FY2024 IFRS operating result was a loss of −€341.3m and net result a loss of −€881.7m [FY24 Annual Report, p.107] — on a clean GAAP/IFRS basis (not the Adjusted EBITDA DHER prefers to headline), the largest scale peer DoorDash is already profitable while DHER's group is not.
- **Source named in:** S&P Capital IQ Competitors export (DoorDash, Inc. matched against Delivery Hero SE (XTRA:DHER), sourced to DoorDash, Inc.'s own 2026 Form 10-K) [`Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Competitors.rtf`]; DoorDash also appears as the acquirer of Deliveroo plc, itself listed in Delivery Hero's own S&P Capital IQ default comparable-company set [`Company-Comparable-Analysis-Delivery-Hero-SE__Business-Description.txt`].
- **One-line read:** The closest scale peer globally, and the only one of the three profiled here that is both GAAP-profitable and expanding into DHER's own regions (Europe, Gulf) through acquisition rather than organic build-out.

### Competitor C — Jahez International Company for Information Systems Technology

- **Ticker / listing:** Tadawul (SASE:6017)
- **Where they compete:** Saudi Arabia food-delivery platform (Jahez brand, plus the Snoonu and other regional apps it has folded in), directly named as a competitor to talabat and to talabat's own HungerStation subsidiary — both live inside DHER's dominant MENA segment [S&P Capital IQ Competitors export: Jahez International matched against Talabat Holding plc (DFM:TALABAT), sourced to Talabat Holding plc's own filing; also matched against HungerStation, Ltd.].
- **Scale:** FY2025 Group GMV SAR 7.2bn (~$1.92bn at the SAR/USD peg of 3.75) and Net Revenue SAR 2.3bn (~$613m) [Jahez FY2025 results, reported via Zawya, "Jahez's net profits decrease in 9M-25" and mid-east.info, "Jahez Reports FY2025 Results With 10.8% GMV Growth", 2026 (web, dated, unverified — Jahez's own results release was not in the data pool)]. Against DHER's FY2025 revenue of approximately $15.9bn, Jahez is roughly 26x smaller — well outside the ~5x comparable-scale bound, included here as a clear regional/segment-specific rival per the selection criteria rather than a scale peer.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 net income attributable to shareholders of SAR 73m on SAR 2.3bn net revenue is a net margin of approximately 3.2%, down sharply from the prior year — reported as a 61.1% year-on-year decline in net profit, which the company attributes to "a deliberate and measured trade-off to invest in retaining customers during a period of elevated promotional activity across the industry" [Zawya and mid-east.info, 2026 (web, dated, unverified)]. Jahez states it "maintained double-digit EBITDA margins in KSA Platforms of 11.9%" at the segment level in the same release [mid-east.info, 2026 (web, dated, unverified)]. Return on invested capital / return on equity: not disclosed in any source available to this agent — not public / not disclosed.
- **Source named in:** S&P Capital IQ Competitors export, "Named by Company," sourced to Talabat Holding plc's own filing [`Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Competitors.rtf`].
- **One-line read:** A much smaller, Saudi-only pure-play whose FY2025 margin compression — explicitly blamed on "elevated promotional activity across the industry" — is direct third-party evidence of the price competition DHER's own MENA segment disclosure has not (yet) had to absorb at the same intensity; DHER's MENA Adjusted EBITDA margin actually rose, from 11.3% to 13.4%, over the same broad period [FY24 Annual Report, p.4].

## 3. Competitive Position

Position vs peers in the dominant segment (MENA): **Holding to gaining**, on the evidence available — DHER does not disclose a market-share percentage for MENA, so this rests on proxies. First, MENA's own Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded from 11.3% to 13.4% in FY2024 even as GMV kept growing, the opposite of what margin compression under intensifying competition would look like [FY24 Annual Report, p.4]. Second, Uber's own CEO placed talabat's Middle East gross-bookings growth (~30% in the prior year) and EBITDA margin (~7%, on a business definition that spans mobility and delivery) essentially level with Uber's own Middle East business, describing talabat as "the leading food delivery player in the market" [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. Third, Jahez — a smaller, Saudi-only rival — reported FY2025 GMV growth of only 10.8% and a 61.1% net-profit decline tied to "elevated promotional activity across the industry," consistent with talabat pressuring smaller players on price rather than the reverse [mid-east.info, 2026 (web, dated, unverified)]. This reads as DHER holding or gaining ground in MENA specifically. The picture is different in the second-largest segment, Asia, which is explicitly **losing** share on the company's own words: "GMV of the Asia segment declined (−7.7%), mainly driven by rising competition in certain regions," with Adjusted EBITDA "flat year-over-year, mainly due to the effects of the competitive environment" [FY24 Annual Report, p.105–106].

## 4. Competitive Shape

The Middle East market — DHER's dominant segment — reads as a **consolidated oligopoly**: a handful of platforms (talabat, Uber Eats/Careem, Jahez, Noon Food, Snoonu, HungerStation — the last two already owned respectively by talabat and Jahez) contest each Gulf country, with talabat itself described by Uber's own CEO as "the leading food delivery player in the market" [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. No independent HHI or top-N market-share disclosure exists in this data pool to size the concentration precisely — this read rests on the small, named set of platforms above, not a calculated index. The global on-demand delivery industry, by contrast, is actively consolidating through M&A rather than organic competition alone: DoorDash bought Wolt (2022) and Deliveroo (2025), and Uber has now agreed to buy the whole of Delivery Hero (announced Jul 16, 2026, expected close H2 2027) [Company Comparable Analysis, Business Description tab; Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. Once that deal closes, the number of large independent multi-country delivery platforms globally shrinks further, reinforcing the oligopoly read rather than a fragmented one.

## 5. Caveat

No DHER-disclosed market-share percentage exists for any segment in this data pool — all "position vs peers" reads above rely on GMV/EBITDA-margin trend proxies and on statements made by a competitor's (Uber's) own management on an M&A call, not on an independent third-party share study. Jahez's financial figures come from web-sourced press coverage of its own results release (Zawya, mid-east.info), not from a primary filing in the data pool — labeled web/unverified accordingly and used only for the smallest, most segment-specific of the three named competitors. No public MENA peer other than Jahez (Careem, Noon, Snoonu are all privately held or subsidiaries that do not separately disclose margins) was available to further anchor MENA-segment profitability comparisons; this would be resolved by a Careem or Noon standalone financial disclosure, which does not exist publicly today.
