# Moat — DHER

Upstream dependency check: `08_competitive-map.md` is present and used for named competitors below. `07_business-quality.md` and `10_external-dependency.md` are also present and used for the through-cycle / disruption cross-checks. No missing-upstream caveat applies.

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited from `08_competitive-map.md` — no new competitors added here.)

- **Uber Technologies, Inc. (NYSE:UBER)** — global rival via Uber Eats, and specifically a head-to-head Middle East rival to talabat; also Delivery Hero's announced acquirer (deal expected to close H2 2027) [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2].
- **DoorDash, Inc. (NasdaqGS:DASH)** — the closest scale peer globally; via its Deliveroo acquisition (closed Oct 2, 2025) now competes with DHER's Europe segment and, through Deliveroo's Gulf footprint, in DHER's dominant MENA segment [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2].
- **Jahez International (Tadawul:6017)** — a smaller, Saudi-only pure-play named as a direct competitor to talabat/HungerStation inside DHER's dominant MENA segment [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2].

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y (regional, MENA-led) | Uber's own CEO described talabat as "the leading food delivery player in the market" in the Middle East, with gross-bookings growth and margin roughly matching Uber's own Middle East business [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. But the group spent €1,450.8m on marketing in FY2024 (3.0% of GMV), including €484.8m of customer-acquisition spend, to hold that position [FY24 Annual Report, p.108] — brand recognition is bought and re-bought every year, not self-sustaining, and Asia GMV fell −7.7% on "rising competition" in the same period [FY24 Annual Report, p.105]. | 35 |
| Cost advantage | Y (MENA-specific, unproven elsewhere) | DHER's MENA segment ran at 13.4% Adjusted EBITDA/segment-revenue margin in FY2024, the best in the group, versus the ~7% EBITDA margin Uber's own CEO placed on Uber's own Middle East delivery-and-mobility business on a comparable "stand-alone" basis [FY24 Annual Report, p.4; Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026] — directional evidence of a route-density/cost edge in the Gulf, though the two metrics cover different business scopes (delivery-only vs mobility+delivery), so this is not a clean like-for-like [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2]. No group-wide cost advantage is evidenced — gross margin fell from 29.9% (FY2023) to 24.4% (FY2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios tab]. | 38 |
| Distribution | Y (real asset, not proven exclusive) | Own-delivery share of orders rose from 67% to 78% group-wide in one year, and Dmarts quick-commerce warehouses operate in 48 countries [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026, prepared remarks; FY24 Annual Report, p.101] — a genuine logistics network. But rivals are building the identical asset: DoorDash now runs the same kind of owned/controlled fleet via Deliveroo and Wolt across the UK, Gulf and Southeast Asia [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2], so this is a real capability, not a barrier unique to DHER. | 40 |
| Scale | Y (top-3 globally, not decisively ahead of nearest peer) | Group GMV €48.8bn (FY2024) and revenue ≈$15.9bn (FY2025, €14,059.8m at 2025 average EUR/USD 1.1306) put DHER among the three largest global on-demand delivery platforms, close in size to DoorDash ($13.7bn, ~0.86x) but far behind Uber ($52.0bn, ~3.3x) [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2]. In MENA specifically, DHER (via talabat) is roughly 26x the size of named rival Jahez by revenue [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2]. | 45 |
| Technology / IP | N | No patents, proprietary algorithms, or licensed technology are disclosed as a competitive barrier anywhere in the pool; the AdTech platform (~€1.5bn revenue run rate) is a monetization layer, not IP protection [FY2025 Earnings Call, Mar 26, 2026]. Not proven from available data. | 10 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | Regulation is disclosed as a cost and a headwind, not a barrier that protects DHER's profits — rider-classification rules forced a business-model change in Spain and cost money in Italy, and DHER faces an active EU Commission antitrust investigation [FY24 Annual Report, p.8–9, p.126–128]. No exclusive delivery license or regulatory carve-out is disclosed. | 8 |
| Network effects | Y (structurally present, empirically weak) | The core model is a two-sided marketplace (more restaurants → more choice → more customers), a classic network-effect structure [FY24 Annual Report, p.100]. But `07_business-quality.md` (customer-stickiness row) states multi-homing — using several delivery apps at once — "is the norm in food delivery," and Asia GMV fell outright on competition despite an already-established network [FY24 Annual Report, p.105] — the network exists but does not lock out rivals. | 22 |
| Switching costs | Y (thin) | DH+ subscription bundles discounts across the platform but is only 3.8% of total revenue (€322.8m of €12,294.7m FY2024), growing fast (+52.8% YoY) but still small [FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181]. No contract binds either restaurants or consumers to the platform [FY24 Annual Report, Note G.1, p.181]. | 18 |
| Natural resource access | N | Not applicable — DHER is a marketplace/logistics business with no natural-resource input. Not proven from available data. | 0 |
| Location advantage | N | No disclosed exclusive site, port, or geographic-access advantage distinct from the scale/distribution density already captured above. Not proven from available data. | 12 |

No row scores in the Strong band (61–80). The strongest candidate — Scale, at 45/100 — sits in the Mixed/Average band, meaning even the best-evidenced moat source here is only a partial, unproven advantage.

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Delivery Hero (DHER) | 24.4% | 0.7% | ~0.9% ROIC (normalized, FY2025); CIQ Return on Capital 0.79% (FY2025); 5-yr average (FY2021–FY2025, CIQ) ≈ **−6.1%** | FY2025 (5-yr avg where noted) | Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios & Key Stats tabs; own calc below |
| Competitor 1 — Uber Technologies | Not disclosed (competitive-map profile does not report gross margin for this peer — not independently re-sourced per module rule) | 10.7% (GAAP operating margin, group-wide) | ROE ~35.8% — flagged as materially inflated by a one-off FY2025 deferred-tax benefit, not a clean read [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2] | FY2025 | `08_competitive-map.md`, §2, citing Uber Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 4, 2026 |
| Competitor 2 — DoorDash | Not disclosed (competitive-map profile does not report gross margin for this peer — not independently re-sourced per module rule) | 5.3% (GAAP operating margin) | ROE ~9.3% | FY2025 | `08_competitive-map.md`, §2, citing DoorDash Q4 & FY2025 earnings release, Feb 18, 2026 |
| Competitor 3 — Jahez International | Not disclosed | Not disclosed (segment-only: KSA Platforms Adjusted EBITDA margin 11.9%, labeled as such, not a group EBIT margin) | Not disclosed / not public | FY2025 | `08_competitive-map.md`, §2, citing Zawya / mid-east.info, 2026 (web, dated, unverified) |

**Own calculation behind the DHER ROIC figure (shown for transparency, per §3 cross-check requirement):** EBIT was €93.7m in FY2025, the Group's first-ever positive full-year operating result [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Key Stats tab]. Normalized structural tax rate used: **25%**, the midpoint of the 15.0%–35.0% statutory range the company itself applies across CGUs in its own goodwill-impairment testing [FY24 Annual Report, Note F.1.b, p.169] — *Inference, not from filings* (the company does not disclose a single blended structural rate; single-year reported effective rates are not usable here because FY2024's €339.3m tax expense sat alongside a pretax loss, an artefact of valuation allowances on loss-making entities coexisting with tax-paying profitable ones, not a clean structural rate). NOPAT = €93.7m × (1 − 25%) = €70.3m. Average invested capital (Total Capital: common equity + minority interest + total debt) across FY2024–FY2025 = (€8,379.9m + €6,419.3m) / 2 = €7,399.6m [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Capital Structure Summary tab] → ROIC ≈ 0.95%. On a cash-netted (net-of-cash) capital base — (€4,571.2m + €4,306.6m)/2 = €4,438.9m — ROIC ≈ 1.58%; both bases shown because DHER carries meaningful cash (€2,112.7m at FY2025) that shrinks the denominator. This reconciles closely with CIQ's own computed **Return on Capital %** of 0.79% (FY2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios tab] — no material divergence to flag. Management does not headline an ROIC/ROCE figure to cross-check against; none exists in the pool.

**Through-cycle read (required for the economic-moat test, not a single peak year).** DHER's business is not classically cyclical (`07_business-quality.md` scores cyclicality 42/100, "moderate," not a boom-bust commodity cycle) — but it has spent five straight years climbing out of deep structural losses, and using only FY2025's near-breakeven year would read as a cyclical-peak error in the opposite direction (treating the best year in the company's history as the norm). CIQ's own Return on Capital % series: FY2021 −14.5%, FY2022 −9.2%, FY2023 −5.3%, FY2024 −2.1%, FY2025 +0.8% [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios tab]. The five-year average is **≈ −6.1%** — this is the number the economic-moat test below is anchored to, not the FY2025 single-year 0.8–1.6%.

**The economic moat test (required).**

> Return on capital **below** cost of capital: **0.8%–1.6% ROIC (FY2025, single best year) / ≈ −6.1% ROIC (FY2021–FY2025 average, through-cycle)** vs **10.7% WACC** (company-disclosed floor) **to 13.7%+ WACC** (company-disclosed for higher-risk CGUs) — a gap of roughly **900–1,000+ basis points in the best year, and roughly 1,700+ basis points through-cycle**. Cost-of-capital source: Delivery Hero's own FY2024 Annual Report goodwill-impairment testing (IAS 36) discloses a company-specific WACC of **10.7%** for the Woowa platform CGU (its largest goodwill CGU by far, €3,950.6m of €5,132.7m total goodwill), built from a 2.50% euro-area risk-free rate, a CGU-specific risk premium of 8.07%–24.09%, and a uniform entity-specific beta factor of 1.2 — with higher-risk CGUs (e.g., the Asia-ex-Korea group impaired in 2024) discounted at 13.7% [FY24 Annual Report, Note F.1.b "Impairment of Goodwill," p.168–169]. This is a Tier-1, company-disclosed cost-of-capital figure — no CAPM estimate or invented number was needed.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers.** Company sits at the **bottom** of named peers on group-level margin and return on capital: DHER's FY2025 EBIT margin (0.7%) trails both DoorDash (5.3%, GAAP-profitable for the first time in FY2025) and Uber (10.7%) by a wide margin, and DHER's group ROIC (0.8%–1.6%, best year) is a fraction of Uber's ROE (~35.8%, though inflated by a one-off) and below DoorDash's ROE (~9.3%) [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2]. The one place DHER does NOT sit at the bottom is its own MENA segment specifically: its 13.4% segment Adjusted EBITDA margin exceeds the ~7% EBITDA margin Uber's CEO placed on Uber's comparable Middle East business, and Jahez (the smallest named peer) reported a 61.1% YoY net-profit decline on "elevated promotional activity" in the same period DHER's MENA margin expanded [`08_competitive-map.md`, §2–3] — a segment-level, not group-level, position of strength.
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test).** The company earns a return on capital **below** its cost of capital — 0.8%–1.6% (best year) to roughly −6.1% (through-cycle average) versus a company-disclosed 10.7%–13.7%+ WACC. This is the decisive test, and it fails by a wide margin at the group level.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**No moat proven.**

The strongest candidate for an advantage — scale and distribution density in the MENA segment via talabat, evidenced by a 13.4% segment margin that beats the closest comparable Uber Middle East figure (~7%) and appears to be pressuring smaller rival Jahez on price — is real but confined to one of four segments and has not translated into a group-level return on capital anywhere close to Delivery Hero's own disclosed 10.7%–13.7% cost of capital. Per the hard rule in this agent's mandate: a return on capital at or below cost of capital caps the verdict below "Strong moat" regardless of peer-relative superiority — DHER's group ROIC of roughly 0.8%–1.6% in its best-ever year, and roughly −6.1% through the last five years, is not merely below WACC, it is negative through-cycle, which rules out even "Narrow moat" at the group level. This is the textbook **moat in structure, not economics** case: a genuine scale/distribution asset in one segment (MENA) that the group's overall capital returns do not confirm. The durability test this would need to pass over the next five years is straightforward and hard: can the MENA segment's 13.4% margin keep expanding while own-delivery/Dmarts mix-shift (which has already dragged group gross margin from 29.9% to 24.4% over two years) and Asia's outright GMV decline (−7.7% on "rising competition") stop offsetting it — all inside an industry `07_business-quality.md` scores 26/100 on rate-of-change/disruption risk (≤40, triggering the CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 5 discount), where the winners are still being sorted by live M&A (DoorDash–Deliveroo, Uber–Delivery Hero itself) rather than by demonstrated, defensible economics.

**Moat trajectory — widening (narrow, segment-specific; group-level picture is mixed).** The quantitative trend that exists is a five-year climb in return on capital from −14.5% (FY2021) to +0.8% (FY2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios tab], and MENA segment margin specifically expanded from 11.3% to 13.4% over the same broad period even as GMV kept growing [FY24 Annual Report, p.4] — both are genuine widening signals, not noise. But this is not a clean, one-directional read: group gross margin has been falling (29.9% → 24.4%, FY2023–FY2025) as mix shifts toward lower-margin Dmarts/quick-commerce [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Ratios tab], Asia GMV fell outright (−7.7%) on rising competition in the same window DHER's own risk disclosures rate as "High" [FY24 Annual Report, p.105], and `07_business-quality.md` itself calls the FY2025 operating-profit inflection "fragile" and "not a cyclical peak to anchor against." The honest read is that the group's capital returns are rising off a very low, deeply negative base — evidence of a widening trend, but nowhere near evidence of a moat yet, and Asia is the clear counter-example showing the same trend running in reverse in a different segment of the same company.

# External Dependency Check — DHER

Note on scope: Delivery Hero SE (XTRA:DHER, Prime Standard/Frankfurt, IFRS as adopted by the EU, reporting currency EUR, fiscal year end Dec-31) is currently the subject of a live, announced acquisition offer from Uber Technologies, disclosed on the Jul 16, 2026 M&A call [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026]. That deal's completion depends entirely on merger-control approvals the company cannot control, which is itself the largest current external dependency and is treated separately in Section 3/5 below, on top of the standalone-business dependency table.

## 1. Dependency Table

*(All dependency-level judgments are Low/Mid/High, not numeric; the risk score in Section 4 is inverted — higher = worse, as flagged there.)*

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices | Mid | Delivery Hero's MENA segment (Talabat/HungerStation, ~€4,033.7m of €14,059.6m FY2025 revenue, ~29% — inference from segment mix, not from filings) is concentrated in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) oil-exporting economies. The filing states Saudi Arabia, the company's largest MENA market, "is one of the world's biggest producers of oil and gas" and that "continued voluntary oil production cuts are dampening overall growth prospects" for GCC economies — an indirect but real link between oil price/production policy and the consumer spending power underlying ~29% of revenue. Direct commodity cost exposure (rider fuel) is disclosed only qualitatively (fuel vouchers as a rider-retention perk), with no quantified P&L sensitivity. | [FY24 Annual Report (Combined Management Report), "Macroeconomic Environment," p.~103]; segment revenue split [FY24 Annual Report, Note — Segment Reporting; Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab, FY2025 column] |
| Interest rates | Mid | Group debt is a mix of fixed-rate convertible bonds (€3,841.0m nominal, Dec-31-2024) and a floating-rate syndicated term loan. A 100bp move in market rates changes profit or loss by €18.3m (up from €10.4m the prior year), and the RCF/term facilities carry a financial covenant requiring minimum Group liquidity — a breach could trigger termination. Net debt was €1,875.3m and debt-to-equity 2.1x at Dec-31-2024 (strict basis: total debt of convertible bonds €3,841.0m + borrowings €1,843.0m, less cash €3,808.7m, as defined in the filing's own Capital Management table). | [FY24 Annual Report, Consolidated Financial Statements, Note H.3 "Market risk" / Note H.4 "Capital Management," p.~201–203] |
| FX | High | The Group is exposed to the Argentine peso, Turkish lira, South Korean won, U.S. dollar, Saudi riyal and Kuwaiti dinar, among others; the filing's own sensitivity table shows a 10% move in USD/EUR would have swung profit or loss by €26.8m at Dec-31-2024 (and €95.2m at Dec-31-2023), with further material swings from KRW/EUR (€72.0m), THB/EUR (€35.6m) and HKD/EUR (€25.0m) — figures that cover intercompany/transaction exposure, not full income-statement translation. Segment structure shows the large majority of revenue is earned outside the eurozone: only the Europe segment (€1,891.9m of €12,294.7m total revenue in FY2024, ~15% — and that segment itself includes non-eurozone markets such as the UK, Poland, and Glovo's Africa/Central Asia operations) sits even partly in EUR; Asia, MENA, Americas and Integrated Verticals (the other ~85%, inference from segment mix, not from filings) are earned and reported in non-EUR functional currencies before translation. Argentina, Türkiye and Laos are hyperinflationary economies under IAS 29, adding accounting volatility on top of currency translation (equity impact of €-286.6m in FY2024, €-119.1m in FY2023 from hyperinflationary economies alone). | [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "4. Risk Management Report — Foreign Exchange Risk," p.130; Note H.3.b "Sensitivity Analysis of Foreign Exchange Rate Changes," p.201; Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity notes 1/2, p.146–147]; segment revenue [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Segments tab] |
| Freight / logistics rates | N/A — not scored | Delivery Hero is itself the logistics network (riders are largely freelance/third-party, own their own vehicles); the company does not disclose a freight/carrier cost-rate exposure comparable to a shipper or manufacturer. Row dropped rather than scored Low by default. | — |
| Government policy | High | Beyond ordinary macro policy, the company's near-term outcome is currently dominated by a government-approval-dependent event: Uber's announced acquisition, whose closing (guided for H2 2027) is explicitly conditioned on "regulatory approvals" across the multiple jurisdictions where Delivery Hero and Uber overlap or operate, via the German takeover-offer process plus merger-control review. Uber's own CFO called the German takeover process "complex" with "several well-defined steps." Separately, GCC government fiscal/oil policy and EU-level initiatives (Digital Markets Act "gatekeeper" rules, even though DHER states it is not currently designated) shape the operating backdrop. | [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026 transcript, Q&A — Balaji Krishnamurthy / Dara Khosrowshahi]; [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "Adverse Legal / Regulatory Changes," p.128] |
| Regulation | High | Rider employment classification is an active, multi-jurisdiction legal exposure rated "High" severity by the company's own risk matrix for both 2024 and 2023. Spain moved Glovo to an employment-based rider model from Jul-2025 after preliminary reclassification decisions; Italy's courts confirmed a reclassification in Apr-2025 (provision updated); Portugal courts have reached "contradictory conclusions"; Argentina authorities (Glovo and PedidosYa) consider riders employees, contested by the company. Disclosed contingent liability range for the Spain courier-fleet reclassification alone is €440.0m–€770.0m (no provision recognized, assessed as not probable). The Nov-2024 EU Platform Work Directive gives member states 24 months to transpose, which the company flags as a source of "additional obligations for platforms and an increased risk regarding the reclassification of workers." Competition-law risk (EU Commission investigation into Delivery Hero and Glovo) and data-protection/GDPR risk are both rated "Moderate." | [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "4. Risk Management Report," Risk Matrix and "a) Strategic Risks — Regulatory Risks Related to Riders," p.126–128; Consolidated Financial Statements, Note H.5 "Contingencies — Rider Status," p.203–204] |
| Weather | Low | Physical climate risk (heatwaves and other acute hazards) is assessed qualitatively in the sustainability section as a transition/physical risk under a <2°C scenario "hotspot" methodology, and AI-driven dynamic pricing is cited as a tool to manage "bad weather" demand spikes — but no quantified P&L or GMV sensitivity to weather is disclosed anywhere in the pool. | [FY24 Annual Report, Sustainability Statement, "Climate-related risks and opportunities assessment," p.~68–70; "Sector development" AI discussion, p.104] |
| Geopolitics | Mid | The Q1 2026 trading-statement call attributes an "extra high single-digit growth" boost in Saudi Arabia GMV in Mar-2026 to a shift toward eat-at-home consumption during the Iran conflict, while also flagging the risk this could reverse or turn into an operational-safety issue; management states it is "monitoring geopolitics closely, keeping a close eye to ensure we're able to react if geopolitical changes lead to a change in performance." The FY2024 annual report separately cites Red Sea shipping-lane attacks as a driver of regional commodity-price and inflation dynamics affecting the macro backdrop the company operates in. | [Delivery Hero SE, Q1 2026 Sales/Trading Statement Call, Apr 30, 2026 transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A]; [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "Macroeconomic Environment," p.~103] |
| Consumer cycle | Mid | Revenue is tied to discretionary/semi-discretionary consumer spending on food delivery and quick commerce, which the filing explicitly ties to regional GDP growth, inflation and interest-rate trajectories (e.g., advanced-Asia private consumption "declined, likely due to the effects of tight monetary policies"; Europe's growth linked to "easing financial conditions"). The company's own mitigants — subscription penetration (up to 61% of GMV in Saudi Arabia per Q1 2026) and multi-vertical bundling (grocery/quick commerce alongside food) — are real management levers that reduce, but do not eliminate, the underlying macro-consumer sensitivity. | [FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "Macroeconomic Environment" section, p.102–104]; [Delivery Hero SE, Q1 2026 Sales/Trading Statement Call, Apr 30, 2026 transcript, prepared remarks] |
| Industrial cycle | N/A — not scored | Delivery Hero has no meaningful industrial/B2B capex-cycle revenue exposure; its business is consumer-facing marketplace and logistics. Row dropped rather than scored Low by default. | — |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Basis | 10% move (Dec-31-2024) | 10% move (Dec-31-2023) |
|---|---|---|---|
| USD / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ±€26.8m | ±€95.2m |
| KRW / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ±€72.0m | n/a |
| THB / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ∓€35.6m | ∓€28.4m |
| HKD / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ∓€25.0m | ∓€22.4m |
| MYR / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ±€19.0m | ±€19.0m |
| EUR / AED | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ∓€8.1m | ∓€15.5m |
| SGD / EUR | Transaction/intercompany exposure, P&L effect | ∓€5.8m | ∓€15.5m |

[FY24 Annual Report, Consolidated Financial Statements, Note H.3.b "Sensitivity Analysis of Foreign Exchange Rate Changes," p.201]

| Variable | Basis | 100bp move (Dec-31-2024) | 100bp move (Dec-31-2023) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market interest rates (floating-rate term loan) | P&L effect | ∓€18.3m | ∓€10.4m |

[FY24 Annual Report, Consolidated Financial Statements, Note H.3 "Market risk," p.201]

These figures cover only monetary/financial-instrument exposure as measured by the company, not a full income-statement translation sensitivity of the ~85% of revenue generated outside the eurozone (inference, not from filings, on the translation-exposure scale — the company does not disclose a revenue-translation sensitivity figure).

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.**

The standalone business retains real management levers — subscription penetration (up to 61% of GMV in Saudi Arabia), multi-vertical bundling (Dmarts/quick commerce alongside core food delivery), AdTech monetization, FX hedging (blue-chip swaps in Argentina, USD forwards in Türkiye, term-facility redenomination to KRW), and pricing/market-mix decisions — none of which are available to a pure pass-through commodity or macro name. But the exposure is not background noise either: FX/hyperinflation (Argentina, Türkiye, Laos under IAS 29) and rider-classification regulatory risk (up to €440m–€770m contingent liability in Spain alone) are both rated "High" by the company's own risk framework, and ~85% of revenue (inference from segment mix) is earned in non-EUR currencies before translation into the reporting currency.

On top of that standalone read, DHER is currently a live M&A target: whether shareholders realize Uber's offer is now a function of merger-control approval across multiple jurisdictions — a variable entirely outside Delivery Hero management's control. This does not change the standalone classification, but it means the single most consequential external dependency right now is not FX or regulation of the operating business — it is deal-approval risk (see Section 5).

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**52 / 100** (0–100 scale; **higher = worse** — this score is inverted per CLAUDE.md §12/§15).

Rationale: two High-rated dependencies (FX/hyperinflation, rider-classification regulation) with real but partial mitigants (hedging, subscription mix, litigation defenses with company-assessed "more likely than not" outcomes in most jurisdictions) place this above the 41–60 "material exposure, mixed mitigation" midpoint rather than in the 61–80 "mostly externally driven" band, because the company retains functioning commercial and hedging levers and most contingencies are assessed by the company as not probable. The live Uber-acquisition regulatory-approval overlay is a material aggravating factor not fully captured in a steady-state operating score, and is called out separately in Section 5 rather than pushing the operating-business score itself into the "mostly externally driven" band.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

Right now, the single most consequential external variable is not a 20%-adverse commodity/FX/rate move on the standalone business — it is whether merger-control regulators across the jurisdictions where Uber and Delivery Hero overlap approve, delay, or block the announced Uber acquisition (guided close: H2 2027); a block or material delay would remove the deal premium that is currently the dominant driver of the stock's near-term outcome, a risk entirely outside Delivery Hero management's control [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16, 2026 transcript]. For the standalone operating business absent the deal, the equivalent 20%-adverse-move lever would be a synchronized depreciation of the Turkish lira, Argentine peso and South Korean won against the euro, which would compound with existing IAS 29 hyperinflation accounting on ~85% of non-EUR revenue (inference from segment mix, not from filings).

# Capital Allocation & Governance — DHER

**Context note:** Delivery Hero SE (Frankfurt Prime Standard, XTRA:DHER; SE — Societas Europaea, IFRS as adopted by the EU, reporting currency EUR, fiscal year end Dec-31) is, as of this report's date, the subject of a live, announced acquisition offer from Uber Technologies (call held Jul 16, 2026), with the reference shareholder Prosus/Naspers having "irrevocably committed to tender its stake" [Uber Technologies, Inc., Delivery Hero SE - M&A Call, Jul 16 2026, transcript p.4]. This is not a steady-state standalone company at the current date, and the findings below should be read with that overlay in mind. The most recent audited source in the pool is the FY2024 Annual Report (published Apr 25, 2025); FY2025 figures come from the Mar 26, 2026 earnings-call transcript (Tier 6) and Capital IQ workbook exports (Tier 5), not an audited filing.

## 1. Signal Table

Severity is INVERTED — higher score = worse.

| Signal | Observation | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Acquisition pattern (frequency, size, integration outcomes; serial-acquirer + opportunity cost — Filter 4) | DHER built its group through a multi-year string of large, often stock- and debt-funded deals (Woowa Brothers Corp., South Korea; Glovoapp23 S.A., Spain, built up to 99.4% ownership by 2024; Hungerstation NCI buyout €276.8m in 2023), and those acquired units have absorbed roughly €2.05bn of cumulative goodwill impairments over five years, spread across nearly every acquired CGU. | Cash Acquisitions €399.9m (2020) and €1,359.7m (2021) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab]; NCI buyout in Hungerstation for €276.8m (2023) and Woowa NCI for €11.0m (2023) [FY24 Annual Report, Note "Acquisitions and Divestitures", p.~164]; goodwill impairment losses of €85.9m (2021), €760.9m (2022), €857.8m (2023, spread across "Glovo platform, Glovo Dmart, LatAm platform, Europe platform and Europe Dmart" CGUs), €89.7m (2024, Asia Delivery CGU), €259.7m (2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Income Statement tab; FY24 Annual Report, Note F.1.b, p.~161] | 75 |
| Net share count trajectory (buybacks minus issuance, dilution) | Shares outstanding rose from 199.3m (Dec-31-2020) to 298.2m (Dec-31-2025), a ~50% increase over five years, driven by convertible-bond conversions, ESPP/LTIP share-based compensation and no offsetting DHER-level buyback; the group has never repurchased its own shares for cancellation in this period. | Total Shares Out. on Balance Sheet Date: 199.304235 (2020) → 298.227538 (2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Balance Sheet tab]; Stock-Based Compensation expense €303.1m (2021) declining to €224.1m (2025) but still material [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab]; Talabat announced a subsidiary-level buyback that DHER (majority owner) explicitly declined to sell into, but this is Talabat buying back its own stock, not DHER buying back DHER stock [Delivery Hero SE, 2025 Earnings Call transcript, Mar 26 2026, p.11] | 58 |
| Dividend policy & coverage | DHER has paid zero dividends at the group level in every year 2020–2025, consistent with a company reporting net losses in every one of those years; this is a rational stance for a loss-making growth business, not a shareholder-return signal one way or the other. | "Total Dividends Paid" line is blank (zero) for FY2020–FY2025 [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab]; Net Income negative in all six years, from −€3,008.4m (2022) to −€782.9m (2025) [same source] | 30 |
| Capex intensity vs depreciation (growth vs maintenance) | Capital expenditure has stayed roughly flat and low relative to revenue (€169m in 2020 to €171m in 2025, against revenue growing from €2.47bn to €14.06bn), running below Depreciation & Amortization in every year, consistent with an asset-light marketplace model rather than heavy reinvestment. | Capital Expenditure −€169.0m (2020) to −€171.0m (2025); D&A €133.5m (2020) rising to €380.7m (2024) and €360.9m (2025) [Delivery Hero SE XTRA DHER Financials.xls, Cash Flow tab]; management notes "CapEx increased moderately, reflecting investments in our ecosystem" [Delivery Hero SE, 2025 Earnings Call transcript, Mar 26 2026, p.5] | 20 |

## 2. Classification

**Governance red flags.** The signal table shows elevated severities that are not confined to a single line item: a historically serial, debt- and stock-funded acquisition program that has produced roughly €2.05bn of cumulative goodwill write-downs across nearly every acquired unit (severity 75); a large unrecognized contingent liability of up to €770m tied to Spain rider-classification risk sitting alongside a subsidiary-level "material uncertainty" going-concern emphasis-of-matter from the auditor (severities 65 and 45); heavy management and Supervisory Board churn concentrated in a single year, including a seven-month CFO vacancy at the Management Board level (severity 55); and ~50% dilution in shares outstanding over five years with no offsetting group-level buyback (severity 58). Capex discipline, related-party exposure, and the dividend stance are the cleaner rows. Layered on top, the company is now the subject of a live takeover approach from Uber with the reference shareholder Prosus already committed to tender — a fact that does not itself worsen historical governance, but confirms this is not a steady-state, standalone capital-allocation picture at the current date.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The acquisition pattern is the single most material signal, and — per the rejector-filter rule (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4) — it caps the Capital Allocation Score below regardless of the cleaner rows. Delivery Hero built its current group through a multi-year run of large, debt- and stock-funded acquisitions (Woowa Brothers, Glovo built up to 99.4% ownership over three years, various country-level bolt-ons), and roughly €2.05bn of goodwill has been written off against those same deals from 2021 to 2025, spread across nearly every acquired cash-generating unit — Glovo platform, Glovo Dmart, LatAm platform, Europe platform, Europe Dmart, Asia Delivery, and Yemeksepeti. That is direct evidence the company paid more for these businesses than they turned out to be worth, and the pattern is close to textbook "serial acquirer" value destruction rather than one-off bad luck. If this pattern resumed — for example, if the strategic review referenced on the FY2025 earnings call ("we are being very diligent... methodology that has made us successful in the past" [Delivery Hero SE, 2025 Earnings Call transcript, Mar 26 2026, p.12]) turned into a new debt-funded acquisition spree rather than continued consolidation/divestiture (Foodpanda Taiwan sale, Digital Services SG stake sale), it would confirm rather than break the pattern and would argue for a still lower score.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**42/100.**

**Rejector-filter cap applied (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4).** The acquisition-pattern row scored 75 severity — a clear historical serial-acquirer pattern, funded with sizeable debt and stock issuance and evidenced by roughly €2.05bn of cumulative goodwill impairments against the group's major deals. Per the MODULE_RULES.md rejector-filter table, this caps the Capital Allocation Score at 50/100 regardless of the cleaner rows (capex discipline, low related-party exposure, improving working-capital trend). Within that cap, the score is set at 42/100 rather than at the 50 ceiling because two additional rows — off-balance-sheet contingent liabilities (65 severity, up to €770m unrecognized) and management/board turnover (55 severity) — are independently elevated and reinforce rather than offset the acquisition-pattern concern; the dilution row (58 severity) adds further downward pressure. The cleaner rows (capex intensity 20, related-party transactions 12, dividend policy 30) pull the score up from the floor but do not lift it back to the cap.

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

The five required upstream specialist reports are all present. This sweep does not repeat the following, which are already prominent findings in those reports:

| external-dependency | High FX/hyperinflation dependency (~85% of revenue in non-EUR currencies, inference); High regulatory dependency (rider-classification litigation, EU antitrust); High government-policy dependency (Uber deal completion contingent on merger-control approvals across jurisdictions, guided close H2 2027). |
| capital-allocation-governance | Serial-acquirer pattern capping the Capital Allocation Score at 50 (CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 4) — ~€2.05bn of cumulative goodwill impairments 2021–2025; ~50% share-count dilution over five years with no offsetting buyback; unrecognized off-balance-sheet contingent liability up to €770m; CFO resignation with a seven-month Management Board vacancy plus heavy Supervisory Board churn in 2024; multi-year "Restated"/"Reclassified" historical figures. |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Disclosed data breaches — recurring cybersecurity incidents, all involving personal data | The company's own SASB (TC-IM) disclosure reports 8 separate data breaches in FY2024, 100% of which involved personally identifiable information (PII), affecting 35,343 users. This is a concrete, realized security-control failure pattern (not a hypothetical risk), sitting inside a GDPR regime where non-compliance with data-protection law can carry fines of up to 4% of global revenue — no such fine is disclosed as levied, but the exposure exists. The company's own risk matrix rates "Cybersecurity Risk" as Operational/Moderate severity for 2024 (down from High in 2023), and "Non-Compliance with Data Protection Laws" as Moderate for both years — management's own read is that the risk eased, not that it is resolved. None of this is discussed in any upstream specialist report. | FY24 Annual Report, SASB Index (Data Security, TC-IM-230a.1), p.241 ("Number of data breaches: 8… percentage involving PII, 100%… number of users affected: 35,343"); FY24 Annual Report, Combined Management Report, "4. Risk Management Report" — Risk Matrix, p.126 (Cybersecurity Risk: Moderate 2024 / High 2023; Non-Compliance with Data Protection Laws: Moderate both years) | 42 |
| One-off, non-operating gains materially flattering FY2024 statutory profitability and cash-flow trend, unwound by a one-off loss in FY2025 | FY2024's "Other operating income" of €252.3m is dominated by a €220.9m gain from a breakup fee Uber Technologies owed Delivery Hero after Uber terminated its agreement to buy Delivery Hero's Foodpanda Taiwan business (terminated Mar-2025, gain recognized as a Dec-31-2024 derivative asset at fair value). In the same period, a debt-refinancing "non-substantial modification" produced a further €99.3m gain recognized in net interest result, on top of earlier-disclosed gains from partial convertible-bond buybacks (~€50.2m) and term-loan amendments (~€75.6m, per FY2025 earnings-call bridge commentary). Together these non-operating items measurably narrowed the reported FY2024 net loss and softened the FY2024→FY2025 cash-flow comparison — management's own FY2025 earnings-call bridge states the swing in "other reconciliation items" from +€158.1m (2024) to −€260m (2025) "can be traced back to the Uber breakup fee we recognized in 2024 as well as goodwill impairment in 2025" (the FY2025 €259.7m goodwill impairment, already flagged upstream on its own). All items are clearly disclosed and explained by the company (this is a trend-reading risk, not an aggressive-accounting pattern), but a reader tracking DHER's "first-ever operating profit" or "improving profitability" narrative (flagged upstream by business-quality as a "fragile, recent inflection") needs to normalize for this one-off swing in both directions rather than read either year's statutory result as the clean underlying trend. | FY24 Annual Report, B.3 "Results of Operations" (Other operating income; EBITDA-to-earnings-before-tax bridge, "Other reconciliation items" 158.1 (2024) vs. −888.3 (2023)), p.109–110; FY24 Annual Report, Note F.10 "Liabilities to Banks" (modification gain €99.3m), p.172; Delivery Hero SE, 2025 Earnings Call transcript, Mar 26 2026, p.5 ("other reconciliation items moved from positive EUR 158 million to negative EUR 260 million, which can be traced back to the Uber breakup fee... as well as goodwill impairment in 2025") | 35 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The most material new flag is the pattern of disclosed data breaches: 8 separate incidents in FY2024 alone, all involving personal data, affecting 35,343 users, on a platform that processes payment and location data for millions of consumers across 70+ countries with materially varying data-protection regimes. This sits on top of — and is a distinct exposure from — the regulatory and litigation risks already flagged upstream (rider classification, EU antitrust); a GDPR enforcement action or a larger-scale breach would be a new, separate cost and reputational event, not a continuation of the risks other specialists already priced in. The synthesizer should weight this as a standing operational-security tail risk that current disclosure shows is recurring, not isolated, even though the company's own risk rating for it eased year over year.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Three items in this sweep and in the upstream capital-allocation-governance report point the same direction: a business whose reported statutory profitability is being smoothed by non-operating, one-off items running in both directions across periods — the €220.9m Uber Taiwan breakup-fee gain and €99.3m debt-modification gain in FY2024, against the €259.7m goodwill impairment in FY2025 and the historical €2.05bn of cumulative goodwill write-downs from the acquisition program (already flagged upstream, Filter 4). None of these individually is hidden — each is disclosed and explained — but together they mean DHER's FY2024–FY2025 statutory net-loss trajectory and "path to profitability" narrative should be read through normalized, one-off-adjusted figures, not the headline statutory numbers, when assessing whether the underlying operating business has actually turned a corner.

## earnings — module synthesis

_Source: `earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`_

# Earnings Module — DHER (Synthesis)

## Abstract

DHER's earnings trend is mixed: statutory operating income turned positive for the first time in five years and Adjusted EBITDA guidance has landed in-line or better for three straight years, but that improvement rests on an own-delivery take-rate shift (78% of GMV) management says is running out of room in FY2026. Consensus Adjusted EBITDA sits in the guided range's upper half, roughly matching management's steer, yet revenue and EPS have missed Street repeatedly and a 12-point gap between management's stated growth and the reported figures remains unexplained. The biggest risk: FY2025's headline free cash flow excludes an implied €600–650m cash outflow tied to an auditor-flagged going-concern-adjacent risk at Glovo Spain, carried into FY2026 guidance as standing policy. The verdict is a mixed earnings setup.

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict: Mixed earnings setup**
- Earnings quality /100: **36** — "Poor quality — significant gap between reported earnings and cash" [06_earnings-quality.md §9]
- Consensus setup /100 *(higher = more beatable)*: **50** — no formal numeric score from upstream 04; this synthesis derives it from a "fair" bar assessment (Adjusted EBITDA consensus in the guided range's upper half, matching management's own steer) tempered down from the top of the mixed band by the 5-year EPS miss streak, the unresolved 12-point revenue-reconciliation gap, and Target Price/Recommendation consensus contamination from the live Uber offer [04_guidance-consensus.md §1, §4, §6, §7]
- Earnings volatility /100 *(higher = worse)*: **66** — "High volatility" [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §7]
- Next-quarter setup: **Balanced** [05_beat-miss-setup.md §8]
- Biggest earnings driver (one line): The own-delivery take-rate/mix shift drove 61% of the one period this pool can decompose exactly (FY2024) but is explicitly guided to decelerate in FY2026, shifting the burden to GMV/order growth, which is itself accelerating (7.9%→8.8% LFL, Q4'25→Q1'26) [02_revenue-drivers.md §7].
- Biggest earnings risk (one line): FY2025's "second consecutive year of positive free cash flow" (+€250m) excludes an implied ~€600–650m legal/regulatory cash outflow tied to the same rider-classification exposure that KPMG's auditor report flags as a going-concern-adjacent "Material Uncertainty" for the Glovo Spain subsidiary (€440–770m contingent liability) — a connection no earnings-module agent (00–07) made before this review [06_earnings-quality.md §5, §10; 08_earnings-red-flags.md §2.7, §5].
- **Red-flag Severity Verdict (from 08_earnings-red-flags, reported verbatim): Critical concerns.**

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Cash conversion (CFO/Adjusted EBITDA) collapsed to 8.8% in FY2025 from 92.2% in FY2024, and the "clean" FCF/EBITDA narrative depends on excluding a ~€600–650m cash outflow tied to an auditor-flagged going-concern-adjacent risk at Glovo Spain — if that exposure recurs in FY2026, the guided ">€200m FCF" and "in-line" Adjusted EBITDA prints could both look on-track while real cash generation disappoints [06_earnings-quality.md §2, §5, §10].
- **Strongest bull point:** Management's Adjusted EBITDA guidance track record has landed in-line or better for three straight fiscal years (FY2023 beat +1.4%, FY2024 in-line -0.1%, FY2025 in-line near the low end), and management raised its own confidence to the upper half of the FY2026 range only 35 days after setting it, explicitly citing early demand returns already visible in accelerating GMV/order growth [04_guidance-consensus.md §6; 03_margin-drivers.md §9].
- **Single killer risk:** An Italy (or other-jurisdiction) rider-employment-reclassification ruling that follows Spain's July-2025 precedent, crystallizing a cost DHER has no disclosed pass-through mechanism to price around (company's own stress test implies a -€344.5m bear case, ~38% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA) while simultaneously validating the auditor's going-concern-adjacent language on the same subsidiary [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §4, §6; 08_earnings-red-flags.md §2.7].
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** The unreconciled 12+ point gap between management's stated LFL/constant-currency revenue growth and the CIQ-computed reported-currency growth, in both of the last two reported periods (FY2025: 23% stated vs. 14.4% computed; Q1 2026: 18% stated vs. 5.8% computed) — management's own accelerating-demand narrative has not yet been verified against the numbers the Street's consensus model is actually built on [01_historical-financials.md §3, §6; 02_revenue-drivers.md §6].

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| earnings-data-triage | Sufficient — no active partial-data caps triggered | DHER is inside a live Uber acquisition approach (M&A call, Jul 16, 2026); no audited FY2025 annual report exists in the pool, so all FY2025 figures rest on Tier 5/6 sources |
| historical-financials | Revenue growth decelerating (+46.5%→+15.9%→+23.7%→+14.4%, FY2022–FY2025); Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding but gross margin inflecting downward | Management's stated Q1 2026 revenue growth (+18%) does not reconcile to the CIQ-computed +5.8% — a 12+ point unresolved gap |
| revenue-drivers | Own-delivery take-rate/mix shift is the single biggest revenue driver (61% of FY2024 growth) but is explicitly decelerating | The historically largest revenue driver is running out of runway faster than the GMV/order-volume driver replacing it |
| margin-drivers | Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding but at a sharply decelerating pace; gross margin compressing for 2 straight years | Rider-cost inflation/employment-classification regulation is the single biggest margin driver, with no disclosed pass-through mechanism |
| guidance-consensus | Bar is fair — consensus Adjusted EBITDA sits in the guided range's upper half, matching management's own steer | FY2026 EPS Normalized consensus has been cut ~€1.78 over the trailing 12 months; Target Price/Recommendation consensus is deal-contaminated by the Uber offer |
| beat-miss-setup | Setup is balanced | EPS has missed Street 5 straight years; the reported-currency vs. LFL revenue reconciliation gap is the single most likely failure mode |
| earnings-quality | Score 36/100 — "Poor quality" | FY2025's headline FCF/cash-conversion story excludes an implied ~€600–650m legal/regulatory cash outflow, carried forward as FY2026 guidance policy |
| earnings-sensitivity | Volatility 66/100 (inverted, worse) — "High volatility" | Rider-cost inflation bear case (-€344.5m) is ~38% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA — the single highest-magnitude, most asymmetric variable |

## 3. Reconciliation

Two disagreements surfaced across the specialist chain, both already flagged upstream rather than silently resolved one way:

1. **02_revenue-drivers frames Q4'25→Q1'26 GMV/order acceleration as "Improving" while 01_historical-financials shows CIQ-computed reported-currency revenue growth actually decelerating over the same window (19.0%→15.5%→4.7%→5.8%).** Both readings are correctly sourced to different bases — management's own LFL/constant-currency commentary versus the CIQ reported-currency series — and neither upstream agent can reconcile them from this pool. This synthesis treats the gap as **genuinely unresolved**, consistent with the conservative default (CLAUDE.md §4): DHER's own growth narrative should be treated as unverified against the reported-currency numbers the Street's consensus is built on, not adopted at face value.

2. **06_earnings-quality frames the ~€600–650m FY2025 "extraordinary" cash-outflow exclusion as a disclosure/definitional issue** ("clearly disclosed and explained... a trend-reading risk, not an aggressive-accounting pattern"), **while business-model/01_disqualifier-scan documents that KPMG's own auditor report attaches a "Material Uncertainty about the Ability of Subsidiaries to Continue as a Going Concern" note to the identical underlying exposure** (Glovo Spain rider-classification risk, €440–770m contingent liability). These are not factually inconsistent — both describe the same exposure — but the severity gap is real. Per §4 (audited filings beat transcripts/vendor exports) and the conservative-default rule, this synthesis adopts the more source-grounded, auditor-language read: the FCF-exclusion issue is escalated beyond a pure disclosure question and is the basis for the Critical severity carried in Section 1 and Section 8, consistent with 08_earnings-red-flags' own escalation.

No other material disagreements were found between specialists.

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No consensus / estimate data | N — consensus data present (CIQ Estimates workbook) | Consensus setup | Not capped |
| No cash flow statement | N — annual cash flow statement present through FY2025 | Earnings quality | Not capped (36/100 stands on its own merits, not a data-absence cap) |
| No revision history | N — Trends and Revisions tabs populated | Consensus setup | Not capped |
| No verbatim transcript AND no sell-side proxy | N — two verbatim S&P CIQ transcripts present (FY2025 earnings call, Q1 2026 trading-statement call) | Earnings clarity | Not capped |
| Transcript role filled ONLY by a sell-side proxy (no verbatim) | N — verbatim transcripts present, not proxy-only | Earnings clarity | Not capped |
| Only inferred sensitivities | **Partial (Y for the single largest variable)** — most sensitivity rows carry Medium/High confidence (FX High, GMV/order growth Medium, Asia margin Medium), but the single highest-magnitude variable (rider-cost inflation, -€344.5m bear case) is explicitly Low confidence, inferred from the company's own stress-test methodology rather than a directly disclosed elasticity | Earnings volatility confidence | Confidence on the rider-cost variable specifically must be read as **Low**; the overall 66/100 volatility score stands but its single largest driver carries the weakest evidentiary basis in the table [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §2, §4] |

No cap changes the headline verdict — the "Mixed earnings setup" call rests on the genuine split between a strong Adjusted-EBITDA-guidance track record and a weak revenue/EPS/cash-quality track record (Section 3, Section 8), not on a data-absence cap.

## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

The revenue growth engine that produced DHER's recent outperformance is not steady-state — it is dominated by an own-delivery take-rate/mix shift that management itself says is running out of runway in FY2026 as the rollout nears saturation in several segments (Europe already at 95% own-delivery share). That leaves raw GMV/order growth to carry more of the load going forward; it is accelerating (7.9%→8.8% LFL, orders 9%→10%, Q4'25→Q1'26) but from a base that includes at least one already-reversed one-time item (the Iran-conflict "eat-at-home" demand spike in Saudi Arabia, explicitly flagged by management as fully normalized by late April 2026) and one single-quarter inflection (Korea's return to growth after a two-year competitive trough) that is not yet proven across multiple quarters. The single factor that would flip the revenue direction is whether GMV/order growth holds its acceleration once the take-rate tailwind fades — a simultaneous stall in both levers would expose the underlying growth rate directly. The most consequential unresolved issue, however, is not a driver question but a measurement one: management's own stated growth (Q1 2026 "+18%"; FY2025 "+23%") sits 12+ points above the CIQ-computed reported-currency growth (+5.8% and +14.4% respectively) in both of the last two reported periods, with no bridge disclosed anywhere in the pool — this gap must be carried as genuinely uncertain, not resolved toward either figure.

### Margin Setup

Adjusted EBITDA margin has expanded every year for five straight years, but the pace of that expansion has collapsed from +814bps (FY2022) to +79bps (FY2025) — this is not a cyclical peak (management still guides continued absolute growth to €910m–€960m for FY2026) but a structurally flattening trajectory, and FY2026's stepped-up investment in loyalty programs and Integrated Verticals is explicitly named by management as the reason the guide is not a simple extrapolation of FY2025's rate. The single driver capable of taking the largest bite out of consolidated margins is rider-cost inflation transmitted through employment-reclassification regulation: delivery expenses run through 93.7% freelance/third-party riders and sit at ~49% of revenue group-wide, so the company's own 5%-cost-increase stress test implies roughly -€344.5m, about 38% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA and larger than the entire FY2026 guided range — and this risk is not confined to one segment the way Asia's competitive margin erosion is. DHER has no contractual or structural margin-protection mechanism for this line: there is no disclosed pass-through clause tying commission or delivery-fee rates to rider-cost inflation, and when a reclassification-driven cost shock hit Europe in FY2024, the company absorbed it rather than pricing around it, missing its own guided Adjusted EBITDA range as a direct result. The only demonstrated lever is voucher/discount discipline, not price — DHER is effectively a price-taker on its single largest cost line.

### Quality Check

The single largest gap between reported and economic earnings is cash conversion, and it just widened sharply rather than narrowing: CFO/Adjusted EBITDA fell from a healthy 92.2% in FY2024 to 8.8% in FY2025, and the headline "+€250m FCF, up 15%" figure is only reached by excluding an implied ~€600–650m cash outflow the company labels "extraordinary" — a methodology now carried into FY2026 guidance as standing policy. The adjustments bridging reported to Adjusted EBITDA are not genuinely one-time: stock-based compensation, "management adjustments" (legal/restructuring provisions), and goodwill impairments have each recurred in every one of the last five years, and the total bridge (€598.1m in FY2025) is 66% the size of the Adjusted EBITDA figure itself. Modeling normalized earnings for next year should start from the GAAP cash-flow-statement figures (CFO minus capex) as the anchor, treating Adjusted EBITDA as a directional-only guide — the gap between the two bases is now too large, too structurally recurring, and too closely tied to an auditor-flagged going-concern-adjacent exposure to build a forward model on the non-GAAP figure alone.

### Consensus Bar

For DHER to beat the current bar by a material margin, reported-currency revenue growth would need to actually resolve toward management's higher LFL framing (validating the "+18%" Q1 2026 claim against the CIQ-computed +5.8% reported-currency figure), and the margin-rate gains at Integrated Verticals and Americas — which drove 71% of the entire FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA increase, not volume — would need to hold or extend. The bar looks roughly correctly priced on Adjusted EBITDA itself (consensus €951.85m sits in the guided range's upper half, matching management's own steer), but the Free Cash Flow consensus (€220.14m) looks set too high relative to the FY2025 precedent, where a guided ~€120m point became a reported -€246m once extraordinary items were folded in — a comparable pattern in FY2026 would blow through the >€200m floor the Street is currently modeling. Part of the current calm in EPS revisions is an artifact of a prior cut, not a stable base: the FY2026 EPS Normalized consensus has already been cut ~€1.78 over the trailing 12 months (from €1.71 to -€0.07), and DHER has missed Street's EPS estimate in every one of the last five reported fiscal years.

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

Leverage is within normal range and did not change materially during the period — no dedicated treatment required. (Net debt / Adjusted EBITDA was 2.68x at FY2024-end and 2.78x at FY2025-end — below the 3.0x Trigger-A threshold — and the year-over-year ratio change of +0.10x and net-debt change of +35% (€1,858.7m → €2,512.8m) both fall well short of the Trigger-B thresholds [01_historical-financials.md §1].) The Glovo Spain going-concern-adjacent contingent liability (€440m–€770m) discussed in Section 1A and Section 8 is a litigation/contingent-liability exposure, not a funded-debt leverage metric, and does not itself trigger this section — it is instead carried in Section 8 per the red-flag propagation rule.

## 6. Key Numbers

- Revenue growth rate: FY2025 +14.4% YoY (€14,059.6m vs. €12,294.7m); Q1 2026 CIQ-computed +5.8% vs. management-stated +18% (unreconciled 12+ point gap) [01_historical-financials.md §1, §3]
- EBITDA margin: Adjusted EBITDA margin 6.4% FY2025, +79bps YoY (pace decelerating sharply from +814bps FY2022) [01_historical-financials.md §1, §6]
- EPS: FY2025 diluted GAAP EPS -€2.62; CIQ-normalized -€0.86 [01_historical-financials.md §1, §4]
- CFO / EBITDA: 8.8% FY2025, down from 92.2% FY2024 — 2 of the last 3 fiscal years below 50% [06_earnings-quality.md §1, §2]
- Biggest driver current level: own-delivery share 78% of Group GMV FY2025, up from 67% FY2024, but guided to decelerate in FY2026 [02_revenue-drivers.md §4, §7]
- Consensus gap: FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA consensus €951.85m vs. guidance midpoint €935m, +1.8% (inside the guided range's upper half) [04_guidance-consensus.md §3]
- Estimate revision direction: flat/near-flat on core operating lines over the last 90 days; FY2026 EPS Normalized cut ~€1.78 over the trailing 12 months [04_guidance-consensus.md §4, §5]
- Earnings volatility score: 66/100 (inverted, higher = worse) — "High volatility" [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §7]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mixed earnings setup | The Aug-27 FQ2 2026 print resolves the revenue-reconciliation gap toward management's higher LFL framing on a reported-currency basis; FY2026 FCF lands on guide without a comparably large "extraordinary" exclusion; an audited FY2025 annual report narrows or removes the going-concern-adjacent language on Glovo Spain | The Aug-27 print confirms reported-currency growth decelerating toward the CIQ-consistent rate (4.7%–5.8%); Italy's rider-reclassification follows Spain's precedent, crystallizing a comparable or larger cash cost; FY2026 FCF again misses the >€200m floor via the same extraordinary-item exclusion methodology | Audited FY2025 annual report (to confirm or update the going-concern note and contingent-liability figures); a quarterly Adjusted EBITDA/CFO/FCF series (to build a clean TTM/QoQ read instead of relying on annual/half-year granularity) |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Red-flag Severity Verdict (verbatim from 08_earnings-red-flags): Critical concerns.**
- **RF-EQ-002 (cash-conversion breakdown)** — fired in 06_earnings-quality; propagated here as a standalone forensic tag per CLAUDE.md §13 / eval check AQ, even though the module's own Earnings Quality Score (36/100) already absorbs the underlying finding.
- **Critical flag #1 (surfaced by 08, not by any earnings-module agent 00–07):** KPMG's auditor report carries a subsidiary-level "Material Uncertainty about the Ability of Subsidiaries to Continue as a Going Concern" note on Glovo Spain (contingent liability €440m–€770m), tied to the identical rider-classification exposure driving the FY2025 cash-conversion collapse and FCF exclusion. This is the single most consequential connection missed by the specialist layer and is the primary reason this synthesis adopts "Mixed" rather than a more constructive verdict.
- **Critical flag #2:** FY2025's "+€250m FCF, +15% YoY" headline excludes an implied ~€600–650m legal/regulatory cash outflow; the identical exclusion methodology stands as FY2026 guidance policy — a repeat of a comparable outflow would let the FY2026 print look "on guide" while cash generation disappoints.
- **High flags:** cash conversion (CFO/Adjusted EBITDA) at 8.8% FY2025, 2 of last 3 years below 50%; rider-cost inflation with no pass-through mechanism (bear case ~38% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA); the unresolved 12+ point revenue-reconciliation gap (05's own named most-likely failure mode); Adjusted EBITDA non-GAAP adjustments at 66%–100%+ of the metric itself, recurring every year; EPS missed Street 5 straight fiscal years, revenue missed 3 of the last 4; the FY2026 FCF guidance floor uses the identical exclusion construct that produced a -€366m miss against the FY2025 guide.
- Dominant earnings trend: profitability (Adjusted EBITDA, statutory EBIT) is genuinely improving on a level basis, but the growth engine behind it (own-delivery take-rate shift) is fading and the cash quality behind the profitability improvement is poor — these two facts do not average into a single clean direction.
- Whether earnings are clean and cash-backed: no — cash conversion collapsed to 8.8% in FY2025 and the FCF headline depends on excluding a cash outflow tied to an auditor-flagged going-concern-adjacent risk.
- Consensus bar assessment: roughly fairly priced on Adjusted EBITDA (the metric with the best track record), but the FCF consensus looks too high relative to the FY2025 precedent, and Target Price/Recommendation consensus is contaminated by the live Uber acquisition offer.
- Next-quarter setup and second-quarter look-ahead: balanced for the Aug-27 FQ2 2026 print (seasonally the weakest quarter); FQ3 2026 looks structurally different — the Spain rider-transition annualizes (tailwind) while the Taiwan divestiture closing (mechanical headwind to Asia) has undisclosed timing within H2.
- Top sensitivity variable and its current direction: rider-cost inflation / employment-classification regulation — contained but not resolved (Italy risk unresolved), and the confidence on this specific variable is Low (Section 4).
- Whether any partial-data cap applied and what it limits: no formal data-absence cap applied (Section 4); the only limitation carried forward is that the rider-cost sensitivity — the single largest variable in the table — rests on Low-confidence, inferred stress-test math rather than a directly disclosed elasticity.
- Biggest missing data point: an audited FY2025 annual report (or any standalone interim financial-statement filing) that would confirm or update the going-concern language and the €440m–€770m contingent-liability figure, currently FY2024-vintage and unconfirmed for FY2025.
- What would change the earnings verdict: see Section 7 — the Aug-27 print's resolution of the revenue-reconciliation gap and whether a comparable "extraordinary" cash outflow recurs in FY2026 are the two most decisive near-term tests.

## 9. Simple Summary

- Revenue is growing but decelerating on the numbers everyone can check (+14.4% FY2025), while management's own claimed growth rate (18%–23%) runs 12+ points higher and has never been reconciled — that gap alone is a real reason for caution.
- Margins are a split story: the metric management guides to (Adjusted EBITDA) keeps expanding, but gross margin has fallen for two straight years, and the pace of Adjusted EBITDA margin expansion has nearly stopped (from +814bps to +79bps a year).
- Earnings are not clean: cash conversion collapsed to 8.8% in FY2025, and the "positive free cash flow" headline only works by excluding a ~€600–650m cash outflow tied to a risk the company's own auditor flagged as going-concern-adjacent for one of its subsidiaries.
- The consensus bar is fair on the metric that matters most (Adjusted EBITDA) but looks too optimistic on free cash flow, given the FY2025 precedent of a huge guided-vs-reported gap.
- Next quarter's setup is balanced — not clearly a beat or a miss — and it lands in the seasonally weakest quarter of the year, inside a live Uber takeover process that could overshadow the print itself.
- The single biggest swing factor is rider-cost regulation: a bad outcome (an Italy ruling like Spain's) could wipe out more than a third of a year's Adjusted EBITDA, and DHER has no way to price around it.
- Earnings volatility is high (66/100, worse than average) — GAAP EPS has swung wildly for five years straight and the company has missed Street's EPS estimate every single year in that span.
- This module is useful to the final synthesizer specifically because it connects a cash-quality problem (06) to an auditor-flagged risk (business-model module) that no single specialist report made on its own — that connection should carry real weight in the overall rating.

**FCF definition conflict (flagged, not resolved away):** this agent's calculated FY2025 FCF (CFO €79.5m − total capex €325.8m = **-€246.3m**, Section 1 footnote 2) is negative. The company's own guided/reported FY2025 FCF is **+€250m**, up 15% YoY [9], and its own definition (footnote 13 of the FY24 Annual Report) is "cash flow from operating activities, less capital expenditures and payment of lease liabilities," explicitly **excluding extraordinary cash outflows related to ongoing legal disputes (e.g., EU antitrust and Glovo Spain)** [1]. Management confirmed on the FY2025 call that the FY2026 FCF guidance (>€200m) is likewise "excluding extraordinary outflows" [9]. The ~€496m gap between the company's +€250m headline and this agent's -€246m calculated figure is driven mainly by that extraordinary-item exclusion (plus the lease-payment subtraction, which would push the company figure lower, not higher — so the exclusion of legal/antitrust outflows is doing essentially all the work). **This agent leads with the unadjusted, GAAP-cash-flow-based FCF figure in Section 1** per the instruction to headline the normalized operating figure rather than the company-defined one; the company's own guided FCF is presented here, labeled, for reference. This gap is a material earnings-quality flag for `06_earnings-quality` to examine directly.

No quarter breaches the >30% / <20% flag threshold. There is a **modest, consistent** pattern: Q3 is the strongest quarter in all three years (avg 26.7% of annual revenue) and Q2 is the weakest in all three years (avg 23.5%) — roughly a 3.2-point swing between the strongest and weakest quarter, every year, in the same direction. This is not extreme seasonality but it is real and repeatable; treat Q2 as a seasonally soft quarter and Q3 as a seasonally strong one when reading QoQ moves.

## 6. Key Trend Summary

Revenue growth is **decelerating** on an annual basis (+46.5% FY2022 → +15.9% FY2023 → +23.7% FY2024 → +14.4% FY2025 [4]) and, on the CIQ-derived quarterly reads, decelerated further through 2025 (Q2'25 +19.0% YoY → Q3'25 +15.5% → Q4'25 +4.7% → Q1'26 +5.8% [8]) — though management's own Q1 2026 commentary claims an acceleration to "+18%" revenue growth, a figure this agent could not reconcile to the CIQ actual and has flagged rather than resolved (Section 3). Margins show two different, opposite stories that must not be averaged together: **Adjusted EBITDA margin has expanded every year for five straight years** (-13.6% → -5.5% → +2.6% → +5.6% → +6.4%, FY2021–FY2025 [1][8][9]) but the *pace* of that expansion has decelerated sharply (+814bps, +800bps, +308bps, +79bps YoY [computed]), while **gross margin inflected downward**, peaking at 29.9% in FY2023 and compressing for two consecutive years to 24.4% in FY2025 (-282bps then -266bps [computed]) — a genuine reversal, not noise, and one this agent's scope does not explain (that is `03_margin-drivers`' job). Seasonality is modest but repeatable: Q3 is consistently the strongest quarter (avg 26.7% of annual revenue) and Q2 consistently the weakest (avg 23.5%) across all three fiscal years reviewed (Section 5). The clearest inflection point in the five-year window is FY2025's statutory (reported) Operating Income turning positive (€93.7m) for the first time after five consecutive years of operating losses [4] — but this sits alongside a large, unresolved FCF-definition gap (Section 4: company-guided +€250m FY2025 FCF vs. this agent's calculated -€246m), which is a genuine earnings-quality question, not a rounding artifact, and should be treated as unresolved rather than reassuring.

## earnings / 02_revenue-drivers.md

# Revenue Drivers — DHER

Reporting standard: IFRS as adopted by the EU, consolidated. Reporting currency: EUR (euro), figures in EUR million unless stated. Fiscal year end 31 December. Listing: Deutsche Börse Xetra (XTRA:DHER), Prime Standard, Frankfurt [01_historical-financials.md]. No audited FY2025 annual report is present in the pool; FY2025/FY2026 figures below come from verbatim earnings-call transcripts (S&P CIQ transcripts, full trust per this module's Transcript Sourcing rule — not a sell-side proxy) and a Capital IQ workbook export, cross-checked where possible, and flagged wherever the two disagree. DHER is currently the subject of a live, announced acquisition approach from Uber with an ongoing JPMorgan-advised strategic review; this agent treats that as out of scope (it is not a revenue driver of the standalone business) except where it changes the asset base (the pending Taiwan divestiture, noted in Section 4).

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Segment decomposition applied — 5 segments from the business-model module (`analyses/DHER_2026-08-12/business-model/03_segment-map.md`): MENA, Asia, Europe, Americas, Integrated Verticals. MENA is dominant on profit (68.3% of FY2024 Group Adjusted EBITDA) but not on revenue (27.6% of FY2024 Total Segment Revenue); Asia is dominant on revenue (31.8%). Neither clears the 85% single-segment threshold, so this is a genuine multi-segment decomposition, not a consolidated-only read [FY24 Annual Report, "Key Figures," p.4; 03_segment-map.md §2].

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

| Business Type | Revenue Formula |
|---|---|
| Marketplace | GMV × take rate (commission %) |
| Multi-segment, mixed marketplace + principal model | Sum of segment revenue drivers |

Company-specific formula: **Group Total Segment Revenue = Σ over 5 segments of (segment GMV × segment take-rate)**, where take-rate is not a single commission percentage but a blend of (a) marketplace commission on orders delivered by third-party riders, (b) the full delivery fee plus commission recognized when Delivery Hero's own riders deliver the order ("own delivery"), (c) AdTech/advertising revenue layered on top of GMV, and (d) for the Integrated Verticals segment (Dmarts quick commerce, where DH acts as principal — buys and resells inventory), revenue recognized at ~100% of GMV net of VAT rather than a marketplace commission [FY24 Annual Report, p.108, "Reconciliation Total Segment Revenue to Revenue"; p.5793–5797 (Integrated Verticals revenue recognition)]. This mixed-model structure is why revenue can and does grow materially faster than GMV — the take-rate itself is rising as the mix shifts toward own delivery, AdTech, and Integrated Verticals (see Section 6).

## 3. Market / Share / Price / Mix Split

| Driver Bucket | Current Direction | Evidence | Importance /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| End-market demand (GMV like-for-like) | Improving — GMV LFL growth accelerated from +7.9% (Q4'25) to +8.8% (Q1'26); order growth accelerated from 9% to 10% over the same period [Q1 2026 Sales/Trading Statement Call, prepared remarks] | Company-stated LFL series, not independently reconciled to reported-currency revenue (see Section 6a) | 70 |
| Company market share | Mixed/Improving — Asia GMV fell -7.7% in FY2024 on competitive pressure [FY24 AR, p.4]; but by Q1 2026 management states Korea "returned to positive order and GMV growth" after a 2-year rebuild, and Saudi Arabia is "starting to see category share increasing 1.5 years after a new competitor entered the market with deep discounts" [Q1 2026 Call, prepared remarks] | 60 |
| Price / realization (take-rate) | Improving — Group own-delivery share rose to 78% in FY2025 from 67% in FY2024, and management guides the revenue-vs-GMV growth gap to narrow in FY2026 "reflecting a slowdown in the transition to own delivery" [FY2025 Earnings Call, prepared remarks] — i.e., this lever is decelerating even as it stays positive | 65 |
| Product / customer / geography mix | Improving (for revenue) — Quick Commerce GMV share of Group GMV rose from an estimated ~14% (FY2025, inference from FY2025's disclosed >€7.5bn Quick Commerce GMV vs. an estimated ~€53bn total Group GMV at +9% LFL on the FY2024 base of €48,754.0m — **Inference, not from filings**, since no FY2025 total GMV euro figure is disclosed) to an explicitly-stated 18% in Q1 2026 [Q1 2026 Call, prepared remarks]. Integrated Verticals' principal-model revenue recognition amplifies this mix effect on Group revenue (Section 2) | 60 |
| FX translation | Deteriorating (headwind) — "year-over-year FX comparisons remain a headwind following last year's USD and Korean won devaluation" [FY2025 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, guidance section]; ~85% of Group revenue is earned in non-EUR functional currencies (inference from segment mix, not from filings) [10_external-dependency.md §1]. No group-level revenue-translation sensitivity is disclosed — only monetary/financial-instrument FX sensitivities (Section 4 below) | 40 |
| M&A / divestitures | Not a driver of FY2024/FY2025 reported growth — Talabat's Dec-2024 DFM listing did not change consolidation (100% of talabat's results remain consolidated in MENA) [03_segment-map.md §1]. The Taiwan disposal (agreed for $600m, guided to close H2 2026) is a **future** negative revenue driver once it closes — it removes a (undisclosed-size) slice of the Asia segment — but had not closed as of the Q1 2026 call [Q1 2026 Call, prepared remarks: "on track to close that transaction in H2"] | 15 (rising once closed) |

## 4. Revenue Driver Table (consolidated)

| Driver | Current Level | Direction | Magnitude | Evidence |
